KineticLangevin/Geometry.lean.title: The transformed kinetic energy
KineticLangevin/Geometry.lean.summary: The phase convention is \((v,x)\), velocity first. The paper's transformation is \(T_{\gamma,a}(v,x)=(v+(\gamma-a)x,-v-ax)\). Its squared energy is the sum of the two squared Hilbert norms. This explicit sum matters: Lean's default norm on a product is a maximum norm, not the Euclidean phase norm used in the paper. The identities below also apply with the underlying Hilbert space equal to an L² space of random vectors.

steps.title: Define the change of variables and its nonnegative energy
steps.body: Set \(y=v+(\gamma-a)x\), \(z=-v-ax\), and \(\mathcal E=\|y\|^2+\|z\|^2\). These are the two coordinates used to expose cancellation in the kinetic drift. The definition transform constructs the pair; transformEnergy explicitly sums their squares. Unfolding the latter leaves a sum of nonnegative terms, which positivity proves without any sign restriction on \(\gamma\) or \(a\). Thus the energy construction is valid before selecting the admissible friction regime.

steps.title: Recover position and velocity
steps.body: Adding the new coordinates gives \(y+z=(\gamma-2a)x\). The proof expands the scalar difference with sub_smul and uses module to normalize the vector-space expression. If \(\gamma-2a\ne0\), multiply by its inverse to recover position. A second identity is \(ay+(\gamma-a)z=-(\gamma-2a)v\), giving \(v=-(\gamma-2a)^{-1}(ay+(\gamma-a)z)\). Lean first proves this vector identity, then rewrites nested scalar multiplication and cancels the nonzero denominator. The hypothesis excludes the singular coordinate choice \(a=\gamma/2\).

steps.title: Bound the position projection
steps.body: The triangle inequality and \((\|y\|-\|z\|)^2\ge0\) give \(\|y+z\|^2\le2(\|y\|^2+\|z\|^2)\). Substituting \(y+z=(\gamma-2a)x\) yields \((\gamma-2a)^2\|x\|^2\le2\mathcal E\). In Lean, norm_add_le supplies the triangle bound; nlinarith combines it with nonnegative norms and the square of their difference. The final rewrite uses norm_smul and \(|c|^2=c^2\), so the squared result does not need a sign assumption on the denominator.

steps.title: Initialize a coupling with equal velocities
steps.body: If the velocity difference is zero, the transformed pair is \(((\gamma-a)x,-ax)\). Its energy is therefore \(((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)\|x\|^2\). The proof unfolds both definitions, removes zero and negation, converts scalar multiplication norms to absolute scalar factors, and uses sq_abs before ring. This is the exact initialization coefficient in the synchronous-position contraction theorem.

steps.title: Read off velocity control and phase energy
steps.body: At \(a=0\), the second transformed coordinate is \(-v\), so \(\|v\|^2\le\|v+\gamma x\|^2+\|v\|^2=\mathcal E\). Lean simplifies the zero scalar terms and invokes nonnegativity of the other square. phaseEnergy separately records \(\|v\|^2+\|x\|^2\), the ordinary squared Euclidean phase norm. Both definitions avoid relying on the product's maximum norm; only the transformed energy contains the mixed position–velocity geometry needed for contraction.

steps.title: Use the actual Euclidean transformed norm
steps.body: Define \(\|s\|_T\) as the norm of \(T_{\gamma,a}s\) in WithLp 2 (E × E). This mathlib type equips the two components with the Euclidean product norm. Its square is exactly transformEnergy, by WithLp.prod_norm_sq_eq_of_L2. Thus the norm, squared-energy calculations, and later triangle inequalities all describe the same geometry. Nonnegativity comes directly from norm_nonneg. The construction applies to a Hilbert space of vectors or a Hilbert space of square-integrable random vectors.

steps.title: Prove the triangle and velocity-projection bounds
steps.body: The transformation is additive: expand the two coordinates and let module normalize the vector identities. After this identity, WithLp.toLp_add turns the transformed sum into a sum in an actual normed space, so norm_add_le gives its triangle inequality. Rewriting \(s-t=(s-r)+(r-t)\) gives the three-point bound needed to insert an auxiliary exact path. To pass from an energy bound \(\mathcal E(s)\le B^2\) to \(\|s\|_T\le B\), use nonnegativity and sq_le_sq₀, then replace the norm square by energy. Applying the same argument to the already proved velocity-square projection gives \(\|v\|\le\|(v,x)\|_T\) at \(a=0\).

steps.title: Project position only at the final endpoint
steps.body: The squared position bound is \(\gamma^2\|x\|^2\le2\|s\|_T^2\). Both sides are squares of nonnegative quantities, so sq_le_sq₀ gives \(\gamma\|x\|\le\sqrt2\|s\|_T\). Division by positive friction yields the exact projection factor \(\sqrt2/\gamma\). If the velocity difference initially vanishes, the energy identity gives \(\|(0,x)\|_T^2=\gamma^2\|x\|^2\). Comparing squares with nonnegative \(\gamma\) proves \(\|(0,x)\|_T=\gamma\|x\|\). These two identities explain why the eventual position theorem loses only one factor \(\sqrt2\), while friction cancels out of its bias floor.

KineticLangevin/Contraction.lean.title: Spectral cancellation and pathwise exponential decay
KineticLangevin/Contraction.lean.summary: This module proves a deterministic theorem for a kinetic difference equation \(v'=-\gamma v-H_tx\), \(x'=v\). The continuous linear operator \(H_t\) is allowed to vary with time but must be self-adjoint and satisfy quadratic-form bounds \(mI\preceq H_t\preceq MI\). The theorem derives energy decay from this differential equation. Constructing stochastic solutions whose difference has these properties and taking an infimum over probability couplings are separate layers.

steps.title: Write the derivative and prove exact spectral cancellation
steps.body:
The transformed derivatives are \(y'=-av-Hx\), \(z'=(\gamma-a)v+Hx\). Thus \(\mathcal E'=2\langle y,y'\rangle+2\langle z,z'\rangle\), which energyDerivative records. Multiplying by \(d=\gamma-2a\) gives

\[d\mathcal E'=2\bigl(a^2\|y\|^2-\langle y,Hy\rangle+\langle z,Hz\rangle-(\gamma-a)^2\|z\|^2\bigr).\]

The proof expands linear-map applications, scalar multiplication and inner products. Self-adjointness rewrites \(\langle v,Hx\rangle\) as \(\langle x,Hv\rangle\), so cross terms cancel. ring verifies the remaining scalar polynomial identity. Clearing the denominator keeps the identity valid even at singular parameter values.

steps.title: Use lower and upper curvature on different coordinates
steps.body: Apply the lower bound \(\langle y,Hy\rangle\ge m\|y\|^2\) and upper bound \(\langle z,Hz\rangle\le M\|z\|^2\). Let \(k=\max\{a^2-m,M-(\gamma-a)^2\}\). Both coefficients are at most \(k\); multiply these scalar bounds by the nonnegative coordinate squares. The spectral identity then yields \(d\mathcal E'\le2k\mathcal E\). The explicit premise \(d>0\) permits division without reversing the inequality. Lean names each quadratic-form and maximum comparison, combines them with nlinarith, then uses le_div_iff₀. This proves the dissipativity estimate from spectral bounds rather than assuming contraction.

steps.title: Specialize to the simple friction regime
steps.body: At \(a=0\), the maximum becomes \(\max\{-m,M-\gamma^2\}\). The assumption \(m+M\le\gamma^2\) gives \(M-\gamma^2\le-m\), so the maximum equals \(-m\). With \(\gamma>0\), the differential bound becomes \(\mathcal E'\le-2m\mathcal E/\gamma\). Lean obtains the general bound, proves the scalar comparison by linarith, and simplifies the maximum. This is the energy exponent; taking a square root later gives the norm exponent \(-m/\gamma\).

steps.title: Differentiate the actual transformed energy along a path
steps.body: Assume HasDerivAt witnesses the two kinetic equations at time \(t\). The linear combinations \(v+(\gamma-a)x\) and \(-v-ax\) inherit derivatives by addition, negation and constant scalar multiplication. The vector normalization tactic module reduces them to \(-av-Hx\) and \((\gamma-a)v+Hx\). The Hilbert-space squared-norm chain rule gives derivative \(2\langle y,y'\rangle\), and adding the two rules produces energyDerivative. No derivative of \(H_t\) is needed: only the value at the current time enters the first-order kinetic equation.

steps.title: Apply Gronwall with an explicitly proved derivative bound
steps.body: Define scalar functions \(F(t)=\mathcal E(v_t,x_t)\) and \(F'(t)=\texttt{energyDerivative}(H_t,v_t,x_t)\), with \(K=2k/(\gamma-2a)\). Continuous paths make \(F\) continuous on the closed horizon, and the preceding derivative theorem gives its derivative on the half-open interval. Spectral dissipativity proves \(F'\le KF+0\). Lean feeds these facts to Mathlib's right-slope Gronwall theorem and simplifies its zero-forcing formula, obtaining \(F(t)\le F(0)e^{Kt}\). The zero additive term is significant: this is exact synchronous-flow contraction rather than a numerical defect estimate.

steps.title: Project the energy estimate to the position difference
steps.body: Suppose \(v_0=0\). Substitute the exact initial energy \(((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)\|x_0\|^2\) into the Gronwall estimate. The position projection theorem gives \((\gamma-2a)^2\|x_t\|^2\le2F(t)\). Combining the two inequalities yields the stated squared version of Proposition 1. The final nlinarith only assembles already proved bounds. Its square root, under \(\gamma-2a>0\), is the paper's prefactor \(\sqrt{2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)}/(\gamma-2a)\). This theorem concerns paths satisfying the explicit ODE; it is not yet a probability-law mixing result.

steps.title: Include the initial time through right derivatives
steps.body: Finite-horizon integral solutions naturally provide a derivative within \([t,\infty)\), including at \(t=0\). The coordinate differentiation proof works unchanged with HasDerivWithinAt: add the two right derivatives, normalize their vector coefficients, apply the squared-norm derivative rule, and sum. The resulting derivative is still energyDerivative. The right-slope Grönwall theorem therefore gives the same exponential energy bound under the spectral hypotheses, without imposing a differentiable extension of the stochastic paths to negative time.

steps.title: Recover the full arbitrary-shift prefactor
steps.body: Write \(d=\gamma-2a>0\) and \(k=\max\{a^2-m,M-(\gamma-a)^2\}/d\). The energy estimate and equal initial velocities give \(d^2\|x_t\|^2\le2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)e^{2kt}\|x_0\|^2\). Lean proves \((e^{kt})^2=e^{2kt}\) using Real.exp_add, proves the square-root square identity from nonnegativity of its argument, and compares the squares of two nonnegative quantities. This first yields \(d\|x_t\|\le\sqrt{2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)}e^{kt}\|x_0\|\). Dividing by the positive \(d\) gives precisely Proposition 1's prefactor and exponent.

KineticLangevin/Dynamics.lean.title: Construct the kinetic integral equation by Picard iteration
KineticLangevin/Dynamics.lean.summary: For existence, the phase product may use its convenient maximum norm. This norm is equivalent to the Euclidean phase norm but is used here only to establish a global Lipschitz vector field. The input noise is any continuous additive velocity path starting at zero. The theorem therefore constructs paths without postulating a reference kinetic process; a full Brownian solution theorem additionally identifies the stochastic noise and its laws.

steps.title: Write the drift in the shared integral-equation sign convention
steps.body: The actual kinetic drift is \((-\gamma v-ug(x),v)\). The shared Picard theorem solves an equation with a minus sign in front of its drift integral, so kineticNegativeDrift stores \((\gamma v+ug(x),-v)\). This sign choice ensures that \(Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^tD(Y_s)ds+(B_t,0)\) has velocity acceleration \(-\gamma v-ug(x)\) and position derivative \(v\). The second noise coordinate is exactly zero.

steps.title: Prove a global Lipschitz constant for phase space
steps.body: If \(g\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(\gamma,u,L\ge0\), write \(R=\|(v,x)-(w,y)\|_{\max}\). Each coordinate difference is at most \(R\), and \(\|g(x)-g(y)\|\le LR\). The velocity component of the negative drift is bounded by \((\gamma+uL)R\) using the triangle inequality. The position component is bounded by \(R\). Hence the maximum is bounded by \((\gamma+uL+1)R\). Lean opens the product maximum, proves the two coordinate bounds, rewrites the drift difference into scalar multiples of differences with module, and combines the nonnegative coefficients. The constant is deliberately sufficient for existence rather than optimized for contraction.

steps.title: Invoke the proved continuous-path Picard construction
steps.body: Let the underlying normed space be complete, \(B\) continuous with \(B_0=0\), and \(T\ge0\). The shared theorem ULA.exists_langevin_integral constructs a continuous phase path \(Y\), with \(Y_0=\text{initial}\), satisfying the kinetic integral identity for every \(0\le t\le T\). The call supplies the concrete negative drift and its proved Lipschitz constant. It packages the noise as \((B_t,0)\), whose continuity follows from product continuity and whose value at zero follows from hB0. This is finite-horizon pathwise existence; Gaussian stationarity, a canonical Brownian law, and full probabilistic chain convergence are not conclusions of this declaration.

KineticLangevin/Coefficients.lean.title: Exponential response kernels and valid Gaussian covariance matrices
KineticLangevin/Coefficients.lean.summary: The functions \(\psi_0(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\), \(\psi_{k+1}(t)=\int_0^t\psi_k(s)ds\) encode exactly integrated friction. The Hessian method also uses \(\varphi_{k+1}(t)=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}\psi_k(s)ds\). Integral definitions avoid division by friction, so zero friction is handled exactly. The module proves their calculus and constructs positive semidefinite Gram covariances; it does not yet construct the corresponding Gaussian random variables.

steps.title: Define iterated response coefficients and prove their calculus
steps.body: The recursive definition chooses an exponential at index zero and an interval integral at a successor index; the two rfl lemmas expose these cases to rewriting. Continuity follows by induction: exponential continuity handles zero, while continuity of the primitive handles the successor. The fundamental theorem of calculus then proves \(\psi'_{k+1}(t)=\psi_k(t)\), using interval integrability and continuity of the integrand. The separate zero-index derivative is \(\psi'_0=-\gamma\psi_0\), obtained from the exponential chain rule; convert and simplification reconcile its scalar expression with the recursive notation.

steps.title: Derive friction balance before dividing by friction
steps.body: Differentiate \(1-\psi_0(t)\): its derivative is \(\gamma\psi_0(t)\), and its value at zero is zero. Integrating gives \(\gamma\psi_1(t)=1-\psi_0(t)\). Integrating this identity once more gives \(\gamma\psi_2(t)=t-\psi_1(t)\). Lean first applies the integral form of the fundamental theorem, then commutes a scalar through the integral. The second proof integrates equality of two functions, distributes the integral over subtraction with its integrability proofs, and evaluates the constant integral. Only after establishing these division-free identities do psi_one_closed and psi_two_closed use \(\gamma\ne0\) to derive the familiar quotient formulas.

steps.title: Prove exact time scaling of every primitive
steps.body: For \(c\ne0\), substitution \(r=cs\) gives \(\psi_{c\gamma,k}(t)=c^{-k}\psi_{\gamma,k}(ct)\). At index zero this is the scalar identity \(-(c\gamma)t=-\gamma(ct)\). At a successor, use the induction hypothesis inside the integral, pull out \(c^{-k}\), and change variables in the remaining primitive; one additional inverse factor appears. Lean uses integral_comp_mul_left, so oriented interval integrals also cover negative \(c\). Substituting \(t=h/c\) yields \(\psi_{c\gamma,k}(h/c)=\psi_{\gamma,k}(h)/c^k\). This is the exact coefficient identity used in mass and particle rescalings.

steps.title: Establish initial values, signs and polynomial upper bounds
steps.body: At time zero the exponential coefficient is one and every primitive is zero. For \(t\ge0\), induction and nonnegative integration show every coefficient is nonnegative, even without a sign restriction on \(\gamma\). If also \(\gamma\ge0\), then \(e^{-\gamma t}\le1\). Integrating once gives \(\psi_1(t)\le t\), and integrating again gives \(\psi_2(t)\le t^2/2\). Lean's comparison theorem receives continuous, hence interval-integrable, functions and the pointwise inequality on the interval. These elementary estimates control the local time-step error without approximating the exponential by an unproved series.

steps.title: Check the zero-friction limit exactly
steps.body: Putting \(\gamma=0\) in the integral definition yields \(\psi_0=1\), \(\psi_1=t\), and \(\psi_2=t^2/2\). The first two proofs simplify the exponential and constant integral. The third uses the integral of the first power. These are identities at zero, not limits inferred from quotient formulas, so no removable-singularity argument is needed. They later turn the kinetic exponential step into the constant-acceleration position–velocity update.

steps.title: Define the Hessian response and its useful factorization
steps.body: phi assigns zero to index zero as an explicit convention and defines positive indices by exponential convolution. Its rewrite lemmas expose those cases. Nonnegativity follows from positivity of the exponential and nonnegativity of \(\psi_k\). Factoring \(e^{-\gamma t}\) out of the integral gives \(\varphi_{k+1}(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\int_0^te^{\gamma s}\psi_k(s)ds\). Lean proves the integrands agree by the exponential addition identity and scalar arithmetic. This factorization expresses the convolution as a product of a continuous exponential and a continuous primitive, proving continuity even though the upper limit and the kernel both depend on time. Every \(\varphi_k(0)\) is zero.

steps.title: Compare convolution coefficients in the correct direction
steps.body: For \(\gamma,t\ge0\), the factor \(e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\le1\) on \(0\le s\le t\), and \(\psi_k(s)\ge0\). Thus \(\varphi_{k+1}(t)\le\int_0^t\psi_k(s)ds=\psi_{k+1}(t)\). The proof explicitly establishes integrability of the convolution and primitive before applying integral comparison. At zero friction the exponential factor is one, so equality holds. In particular \(\varphi_2\le\psi_2\), correcting the opposite ordering printed in the supplied Proposition 3; both coefficients can still be bounded above by \(t^2/2\).

steps.title: A Gram quadratic form is an integral of a square
steps.body:
Given continuous scalar kernels \(k_i\), define \(C_{ij}=\int_0^hk_i(t)k_j(t)dt\). Commutativity proves symmetry. For a finite coefficient vector \(z\), expand the quadratic form and interchange its finite sums with integrals:

\[\sum_{i,j}z_iC_{ij}z_j=\int_0^h\left(\sum_i z_ik_i(t)\right)^2dt.\]

Lean supplies interval-integrability witnesses for each product, pulls scalar factors inside, applies integral_finsetSum twice, and normalizes the finite-sum expansion. For \(h\ge0\) the integral is nonnegative. Combining symmetry with this quadratic-form bound proves positive semidefiniteness. This is a matrix property, not yet an identification with Itô covariance.

steps.title: Instantiate the first- and second-order noise covariances
steps.body: The first integrator uses kernels \((\psi_0,\psi_1)\); the Hessian integrator uses \((\psi_0,\psi_1,\varphi_2,\varphi_3)\). klmcKernels and klmc2Kernels list them on \(\mathrm{Fin}(2)\) and \(\mathrm{Fin}(4)\). Their covariance definitions apply the same Gram construction. Finite case splits reduce kernel continuity to the proved coefficient continuity. Each final positive-semidefinite theorem is then a direct application of the general Gram result. In the stochastic algorithm the noise is additionally required to be centered jointly Gaussian with these covariances, independent across time and coordinates; those law properties are not encoded by matrix positivity alone.

steps.title: Strict positivity of every positive-time response
steps.body: For \(t>0\), every response coefficient \(\psi_k(t)\) is strictly positive. The exponential base case is positive at every time. At a successor, the integrand is continuous and nonnegative on the interval, and the induction hypothesis makes it strictly positive at the right endpoint. Mathlib's positive-integral theorem then gives a positive primitive. The proof explicitly supplies both the pointwise nonnegative bound and an endpoint witnessing positivity. No positive-friction hypothesis is needed because an exponential remains positive even when its exponent grows.

steps.title: All higher responses are bounded by their frictionless Taylor coefficient
steps.body: At zero friction induction gives \(\psi_{0,k}(t)=t^k/k!\). Integrating the induction hypothesis uses \(\int_0^ts^kds=t^{k+1}/(k+1)\), and the factorial recursion \((k+1)!=(k+1)k!\) matches the denominator. For nonnegative friction and time, compare each \(\psi_{\gamma,k}\) with its zero-friction counterpart. The exponential comparison starts the induction, and integral monotonicity preserves it at each successor. Substitution of the exact zero-friction identity yields \(0\le\psi_{\gamma,k}(t)\le t^k/k!\). These estimates provide every higher-order coefficient bound without a formal power-series approximation.

steps.title: Evaluate the first Hessian response without division
steps.body: The convolution of the two exponential responses has a constant integrand: \(e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\psi_0(s)=e^{-\gamma t}\). Hence \(\varphi_1(t)=t\psi_0(t)\). Reversing the integration variable also gives \(\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}ds=\psi_1(t)\). To compute the next balance, multiply the \(\varphi_2\) integrand by \(\gamma\), substitute \(\gamma\psi_1(s)=1-\psi_0(s)\), and simplify the exponential product. Integrating yields \(\gamma\varphi_2(t)=\psi_1(t)-t\psi_0(t)\). Lean proves equality of the integrand functions, commutes constants through integrals, and evaluates the constant integral. These identities remain valid at zero friction.

steps.title: Compute covariance entries and the exact friction–noise balance
steps.body: The velocity variance coefficient is \(C_{00}=\int_0^he^{-2\gamma t}dt=\psi_{2\gamma,1}(h)\), proved by combining exponentials. Since \((\psi_1^2/2)'=\psi_0\psi_1\) and \(\psi_1(0)=0\), the fundamental theorem gives \(C_{01}=\psi_1(h)^2/2\). Finally the friction identity at rate \(2\gamma\) yields \(2\gamma C_{00}=1-e^{-2\gamma h}\). Therefore \(\psi_0(h)^2+2\gamma C_{00}=1\), the exact stationary velocity variance balance. Lean proves the exponential square identity and reduces the final expression with ring. An independent unit-variance input velocity and the specified Gaussian noise consequently retain unit variance after the linear thermostat part.

steps.title: Relate the second-order coefficients with an exact integrated balance
steps.body: The derivative of \((t-s)\psi_1(s)+\psi_2(s)\), with \(t\) fixed, is \((t-s)\psi_0(s)\). Integrating and reversing the variable yields \(\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}s\,ds=\psi_2(t)\). Next put the defining integrals for \(\varphi_2\) and \(\varphi_3\) under one integral. The identity \(\psi_1(s)+\gamma\psi_2(s)=s\) simplifies their integrand, giving \(\varphi_2(t)+\gamma\varphi_3(t)=\psi_2(t)\). Lean explicitly supplies interval-integrability before combining the integrals and uses linear_combination for the scalar integrand equality. For nonnegative friction and time, \(\gamma\varphi_3(t)\ge0\), hence \(\varphi_2(t)\le\psi_2(t)\). This provides a direct corrected coefficient relation, rather than the reversed intermediate inequality printed in the supplied manuscript.

KineticLangevin/Integrator.lean.title: One shared exponential integrator and the Hessian correction
KineticLangevin/Integrator.lean.summary: The deterministic maps accept a force vector field and supplied noise vectors. Keeping the force explicit permits particle and inverse-mass reuse. Throughout the module, the first phase coordinate is velocity and the second is position. The coefficient library specifies the covariance matrices required by the probabilistic interpretation; these definitions by themselves make no assertion that arbitrary noise inputs have those laws.

steps.title: Define phase space and the frozen-force step
steps.body:
PhaseSpace E is the pair \(E\times E\). For supplied additive innovation \((n_v,n_x)\), define

\[v^+=\psi_0v-\psi_1g(x)+n_v,\qquad x^+=x+\psi_1v-\psi_2g(x)+n_x.\]

exponentialStep implements these two expressions. klmcStep passes innovation \(\sqrt{2\gamma}(\xi,\xi')\), matching the paper's noise normalization. The velocity and position projection theorems are definitional equalities: rfl exposes the corresponding pair coordinate. This separation lets KIPLMC1 use exactly this implementation with its own temperature amplitude rather than copying the formula.

steps.title: Check zero time and cancel shared additive noise
steps.body:
At zero time, \(\psi_0=1\), \(\psi_1=\psi_2=0\); with zero innovation the step is the identity. Lean proves equality of pairs by coordinate extensionality and simplification. For two starting phases driven by the same innovation, subtraction cancels each additive noise term before any estimate:

\[\Delta v^+=\psi_0\Delta v-\psi_1\Delta g,\quad \Delta x^+=\Delta x+\psi_1\Delta v-\psi_2\Delta g.\]

The proof expands pair subtraction, distributes scalar multiplication across differences, and uses abel for the additive group rearrangement. The KLMC cancellation theorem reuses this exact identity with the scaled noise argument. It does not need Gaussianity.

steps.title: Include every Hessian correction, including noise multipliers
steps.body: With \(H=\nabla^2f(x)\), the second-order map subtracts \(\varphi_2Hv\) from velocity and \(\varphi_3Hv\) from position. Its innovations are \(\sqrt{2\gamma}(\xi_0-H\xi_2)\) and \(\sqrt{2\gamma}(\xi_1-H\xi_3)\). The definition klmc2Step includes all four terms. With zero Hessian, the deterministic and random corrections vanish and the map becomes the original KLMC map using \((\xi_0,\xi_1)\). Pair extensionality and simplification prove this reduction. When comparing two nonzero Hessians, the noise terms differ too; this explicit map prevents silently discarding that contribution.

steps.title: The frictionless map is constant acceleration
steps.body: At \(\gamma=0\), the coefficient identities give \(\psi_0=1\), \(\psi_1=h\), \(\psi_2=h^2/2\), while \(\sqrt{2\gamma}=0\). Therefore \(v^+=v-hg(x)\) and \(x^+=x+hv-h^2g(x)/2\). The proof simplifies the actual map with the exact zero-friction coefficient lemmas. It asserts exact integration of a frozen force, not exact integration of a spatially varying Hamiltonian force along the whole interval.

steps.title: Iterate a prescribed stream of innovations
steps.body: klmcChain starts at the supplied phase and recursively applies klmcStep with innovation number \(k\). Its zero and successor equations are definitional equalities, providing reliable rewrite points for later induction and law identification. klmc2Chain uses the same recursion pattern with the four-block innovation required by klmc2Step. A prescribed noise stream is a pathwise object: assigning independent Gaussian coordinate laws and proving finite moments of this recursion is the next probabilistic task, not a hidden assumption in the definitions.

steps.title: Verify that the frozen deterministic response solves its differential equations
steps.body: For constant force \(g\), define \(v_t=\psi_0(t)v_0-\psi_1(t)g\) and \(x_t=x_0+\psi_1(t)v_0-\psi_2(t)g\). The coefficient derivative identities immediately give \(x'_t=v_t\). For velocity they give \(v'_t=-\gamma\psi_0(t)v_0-\psi_0(t)g\). Substituting \(\gamma\psi_1=1-\psi_0\) proves this equals \(-\gamma v_t-g\). Lean builds the vector derivatives from the scalar coefficient derivatives and rewrites the friction balance before normalizing scalar actions. exponentialStep_eq_frozen is then a definitional equality: the deterministic step evaluates these exact frozen responses at \(h\) and adds the supplied noise. Thus the term “exponential integrator” is supported by an actual ODE identity.

KineticLangevin/OBABO.lean.title: The OBABO splitting and its exact pathwise identities
KineticLangevin/OBABO.lean.summary: OBABO brackets a kick–drift–kick Hamiltonian step between two Ornstein–Uhlenbeck half steps. The module proves the composition and its reversal and cancellation identities for arbitrary supplied vectors. The Gaussian-law and convergence analysis is separate. Its thermostat coefficient is chosen so that the damping and fresh noise exactly preserve a target scalar velocity variance.

steps.title: Define each subflow and compose O–B–A–B–O
steps.body: In velocity–position ordering, \(O(v,x)=(\delta v+\sigma\xi,x)\), \(B_h(v,x)=(v-hg(x),x)\), and \(A_h(v,x)=(v,x+hv)\). obaboStep composes \(O,B_{h/2},A_h,B_{h/2},O\), using distinct noise arguments in the two thermostat steps. Expanding the nested definitions gives \(v_{1/2}=\delta v+\sigma\xi-hg(x)/2\), \(x^+=x+hv_{1/2}\), and \(v^+=\delta(v_{1/2}-hg(x^+)/2)+\sigma\xi'\). obaboStep_expanded is proved by rfl because this formula follows directly from the composition; the new-position force is structurally enforced.

steps.title: Reverse the deterministic kick and drift
steps.body: The kick leaves position fixed, so subtracting \(hg(x)\) and then adding it cancels exactly. The drift leaves velocity fixed, so adding \(hv\) and then subtracting it also cancels. Their inverse formulas hold for arbitrary real \(h\) and arbitrary force, with no smoothness assumption. reverseVelocity negates velocity and keeps position; applying it twice is the identity. Conjugating a kick or drift by this reversal changes \(h\) to \(-h\). The proofs use pair extensionality and simplification of scalar signs, making the time-reversal algebra explicit.

steps.title: The palindromic Hamiltonian composition has an exact inverse
steps.body: verletStep is \(B_{h/2}A_hB_{h/2}\). To invert it, reverse the order and invert each factor. Since the composition is palindromic, this is precisely \(B_{-h/2}A_{-h}B_{-h/2}\). Lean expands the two compositions, rewrites \((-h)/2=-(h/2)\), and cancels the three adjacent inverse pairs with the preceding lemmas. The OBABO zero-time theorem separately checks that \(h=0,\delta=1,\sigma=0\) makes every substep the identity. Reversal of the deterministic map alone does not assert reversibility of a stochastic transition with a particular probability density.

steps.title: Synchronous noises cancel while the new forces remain
steps.body: Apply two OBABO steps with the same \(\xi,\xi'\). The difference of half velocities is \(a=\delta\Delta v-h(g(x)-g(y))/2\). Thus \(\Delta x^+=\Delta x+ha\). The final shared refresh cancels too, leaving \(\Delta v^+=\delta(a-h(g(x^+)-g(y^+))/2)\). Lean unfolds all subflows, proves the velocity and position identities as a conjunction, and normalizes vector expressions with module. Although additive noises disappear explicitly from the difference, the new positions still depend on the common first noise. The identity preserves their force evaluations instead of treating them as old-position gradients.

steps.title: Choose damping and prove the thermal variance identity
steps.body: The OU half-step damping is \(\delta=e^{-\gamma h/2}>0\). The exponential addition identity gives \(\delta^2=e^{-\gamma h}\). With \(\gamma,h\ge0\), this is at most one, so \(s^2=1-\delta^2\ge0\). For a target velocity variance \(u\ge0\), set \(\sigma=\sqrt{u(1-\delta^2)}\). Then \(\delta^2u+\sigma^2=u\). Lean proves positivity directly from exp_pos, rewrites the square with exp_add, uses the nonpositive exponent to bound the exponential, and finally applies Real.sq_sqrt followed by ring. For independent centered input velocity and fresh Gaussian noise this is the scalar covariance balance; Gaussian-law preservation additionally uses those distributional facts.

KineticLangevin/Gaussian.lean.title: Construct correlated Gaussian blocks and an independent noise stream
KineticLangevin/Gaussian.lean.summary: A covariance matrix alone is insufficient to define a random algorithm. This module constructs actual centered finite-dimensional Gaussian probability measures with the Gram covariance and an infinite product giving one independent block per time and spatial coordinate. Correlation is retained within each block. The exact covariance theorem requires a nonnegative step and continuous kernels; the general Gaussian constructor remains a probability measure even outside that parameter regime.

steps.title: Construct the centered Gaussian probability measure and its vector moments
steps.body: For a finite kernel index set, kernelGaussian is Mathlib's multivariate Gaussian with mean zero and the defined Gram matrix. The named instances establish Gaussianity and total probability mass using the distribution constructor. The mean theorem computes its vector expectation as zero, and kernelGaussian_memLp invokes the finite Gaussian second-moment theorem. These are derived properties of a specified probability measure, rather than moment fields of an abstract noise source. They hold even if the covariance argument is degenerate; identifying its entries with the requested matrix uses the positive-semidefinite theorem below.

steps.title: Evaluate coordinate means, moments and exact covariances
steps.body:
Each coordinate projection is a continuous linear functional. Commuting it with the vector integral proves zero coordinate mean, and composing the finite-second-moment identity with that functional proves coordinate L² integrability. For continuous kernels and \(h\ge0\), Gram positivity permits the multivariate-Gaussian covariance formula:

\[\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)=\int_0^hk_i(t)k_j(t)dt,\quad \operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\int_0^hk_i(t)^2dt.\]

The two distribution theorems receive the already proved positive-semidefinite matrix witness. The variance proof only rewrites a product as a square. This identifies the exact correlated coordinate law required by the integrators, while its representation as actual Brownian stochastic integrals is a separate identity.

steps.title: Instantiate the two-block and four-block kinetic laws
steps.body: klmcGaussian uses the kernel vector \((\psi_0,\psi_1)\); klmc2Gaussian uses \((\psi_0,\psi_1,\varphi_2,\varphi_3)\). They are therefore concrete measures on two- and four-dimensional Euclidean space. Each probability instance unfolds the specialization and reuses the general Gaussian probability instance. The first law correlates a coordinate's velocity and position increments; the second also couples the Hessian-correction integrals. Separate spatial coordinates will use separate copies of these entire blocks, rather than separate copies of their individual components.

steps.title: Build one independent Gaussian block for each time and coordinate
steps.body: The path space is \(\Omega=(\mathbb R^{\iota})^{\mathbb N\times\mathrm{Fin}(d)}\). Define its law as the infinite product of the kernel Gaussian. Evaluation at \((n,i)\) is measurable and has exactly the original Gaussian law, by the infinite-product marginal theorem. The coordinate-evaluation family is jointly independent by iIndepFun_infinitePi. Thus a time step retains all within-block covariance while distinct iteration–coordinate pairs are independent. The product's probability instance establishes total mass one; the HasLaw proof records both measurability and the exact pushforward equality.

steps.title: Transfer block moments and assemble Euclidean innovations
steps.body: Evaluation on the infinite product is measure preserving, so composing the finite-block L² identity with evaluation gives a finite second moment for each block. Its expectation is zero by the established HasLaw integral transformation. klmcInnovation collects component zero across spatial coordinates into velocity and component one into position. klmc2Innovation similarly collects each of the four components into a Euclidean vector. WithLp.toLp equips the coordinate functions with the Euclidean norm. Their measurable-map theorems unfold these finite coordinate constructions and apply compositional measurability. These maps supply concrete innovation streams for pathwise integrator recursions.

steps.title: Turn covariance into actual second and cross moments
steps.body: The Gaussian coordinates have zero mean. Thus their variance equals \(\int X_i^2\), and their covariance equals \(\int X_iX_j\). The second-moment proof starts from the exact variance formula, rewrites variance as the integral of the centered square, and substitutes the proved zero mean. The cross-moment proof unfolds covariance and substitutes both zero means. Each conclusion is an equality for the actual constructed Gaussian measure: \(\mathbb E X_i^2=\int_0^hk_i^2\) and \(\mathbb E X_iX_j=\int_0^hk_ik_j\). These formulas can be used in numerical-error calculations without assuming moments of an unspecified noise source.

steps.title: The scalar KLMC transition is an actual Gaussian pushforward
steps.body: klmcScalarTransition maps the constructed correlated two-dimensional Gaussian through the scalar KLMC step at a fixed phase state. The map is continuous in its innovation, so the pushforward remains a probability measure. Both output coordinates are a constant frozen-force response plus \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\) times a Gaussian coordinate. Their finite second moments follow by adding a constant L² function to a scalar multiple of the proved Gaussian L² coordinate. To compute the transition mean, change variables through the pushforward, integrate the two coordinates separately using their established integrability, and substitute zero Gaussian means. The result is exactly the frozen deterministic position–velocity pair. This is a genuine one-step law and moment result, with no assumption that an abstract transition has the desired mean.

steps.title: Correlated transition covariance and independent initialization
steps.body:
The actual scalar phase transition retains covariance \(2\gamma C_{01}\) between its velocity and position coordinates. Lean pulls covariance through the transition pushforward, removes the deterministic means, moves both factors \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\) outside covariance, and uses the Gaussian Gram-covariance theorem; their product is \(2\gamma\) when friction is nonnegative. This checks the correlation in the update rather than replacing the two noises by independent draws.

To initialize independently, the canonical probability space is the product \(\mu_0\otimes Q\), where \(Q\) is the countable independent Gaussian-block path measure. The first projection has law \(\mu_0\), the second projection has law \(Q\), and the two projections are independent. Lean constructs this product explicitly, obtains probability from the two probability instances, and applies the product-marginal and independent-projection theorems. No later-time independence or convergence inequality is assumed by this construction.

KineticLangevin/LocalError.lean.title: Derive the actual frozen-force local defect
KineticLangevin/LocalError.lean.summary: The velocity defect is an explicit exponentially weighted integral of the changing force; the position defect is its primitive. Bounds follow from a Lipschitz force and a kinematic identity, not from a built-in defect hypothesis. The ambient norm may represent a deterministic Banach path or an L² random-vector norm. A kinetic stationarity theorem supplying the required velocity-moment bound remains separate.

steps.title: Define the force-freezing remainder as an integral
steps.body: Set \(D_v(t)=\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}(g(x_s)-g(x_0))ds\), and \(D_x(t)=\int_0^tD_v(s)ds\). These are exactly the terms left when one compares an exact kinetic equation with a frozen-force interpolation driven by the same additive noise. velocityDefect and positionDefect define those vector-valued interval integrals. The definitions impose no desired error estimate. Interpreting them as a numerical-process difference additionally requires deriving the variation-of-constants identity for that process.

steps.title: Integrating velocity gives a linear position increment
steps.body: Assume \(x_t-x_0=\int_0^tv_sds\), with \(\|v_s\|\le C\) on the horizon. The norm-of-integral bound gives \(\|x_t-x_0\|\le C|t|=Ct\) for nonnegative time. Lean rewrites with the actual kinematic identity, applies the constant bound on the interval integral, and translates membership in the unoriented integration interval into \(0\le s\le t\le T\). This is the extra position regularity that kinetic Langevin gains from integrating velocity instead of receiving direct Brownian position noise.

steps.title: Integrate a linear force increment to obtain the quadratic velocity defect
steps.body: Lipschitzness gives \(\|g(x_s)-g(x_0)\|\le MCs\). With \(\gamma\ge0\) and \(s\le t\), the exponential kernel is between zero and one, so the norm of the weighted integrand is still at most \(MCs\). The proof derives this pointwise estimate from the preceding increment theorem, explicit exponential positivity and the norm of scalar multiplication. A continuous scalar majorant provides the required interval integrability. Integrating the bound gives \(\|D_v(t)\|\le\int_0^tMCsds=MCt^2/2\); Lean evaluates the integral and normalizes its coefficients with ring.

steps.title: Integrate once more to obtain the cubic position defect
steps.body: Apply the proved velocity-defect bound at each intermediate time \(s\): \(\|D_v(s)\|\le MCs^2/2\). Its continuous scalar majorant is integrable, so the norm of the position-defect integral is bounded by \(\int_0^tMCs^2/2\,ds=MCt^3/6\). Lean first verifies that every intermediate time stays in the original horizon, rewrites the scalar coefficient into the majorant's form, applies norm-integral comparison, and uses integral_pow. The integration variable inside the bound is \(s\), preserving the correct cubic constant. No stationarity or Gaussian moment is assumed implicitly by this deterministic estimate.

steps.title: Recover the paper’s three-quarter transformed local constant
steps.body: Put \(B=MCh^2\). The component bounds give \(\|D_v\|\le B/2\) and \(\|D_x\|\le Bh/6\). If \(\gamma h\le1/4\), then \(\|D_v+\gamma D_x\|\le B/2+B/24=13B/24\). The transformed energy at parameter zero is \(\|D_v+\gamma D_x\|^2+\|D_v\|^2\), which is at most \(((13/24)^2+1/4)B^2\le(3B/4)^2\). Lean keeps all quantities nonnegative, squares each norm bound with sq_le_sq₀, unfolds the transformed energy and verifies the rational comparison by nlinarith. This derives the constant for the explicit defect integrals; identifying them with an actual stationary-chain coupling still requires the kinetic process construction and moment estimates.

KineticLangevin/PotentialContraction.lea.title: Nonlinear kinetic contraction directly from strong convexity and smoothness
KineticLangevin/PotentialContraction.lea.summary: The spectral proof can be replaced by a sector inequality for an actual gradient difference. This avoids selecting a time-varying averaged Hessian and only needs a differentiable strongly convex potential with Lipschitz gradient. The module proves the simple \(\sqrt2e^{-mt/\gamma}\) pathwise position estimate from the concrete noise-cancelled equations. Stochastic solution construction and Wasserstein law comparison are separate steps.

steps.title: Write the concrete energy derivative and the gradient sector inequality
steps.body: For velocity difference \(v\), position difference \(x\), and force difference \(g\), define \(D=2\langle v+\gamma x,-g\rangle+2\langle-v,\gamma v+g\rangle\). The strong-smooth interpolation inequality is \(mM\|x\|^2+\|g\|^2\le(m+M)\langle g,x\rangle\). Subtract the linear part \(mx\), expand its squared norm, and rearrange to obtain \(\|g-mx\|^2\le(M-m)\langle x,g-mx\rangle\). Lean performs this expansion with the Hilbert norm-square and inner-product identities, then uses nlinarith. This sector estimate contains the joint lower–upper curvature information needed for contraction.

steps.title: Complete a square to prove dissipativity
steps.body:
Put \(k=g-mx\). Expanding the transformed energy yields

\[\gamma D+2m\mathcal E =2\bigl[-(\gamma^2-2m)\|v\|^2-2\gamma\langle v,k\rangle-\gamma^2\langle x,k\rangle\bigr].\]

When \(M=m\), the sector inequality forces \(k=0\); friction gives \(\gamma^2\ge2m\), proving nonpositivity. When \(M>m\), combine the sector estimate with \(\|\gamma k+(M-m)v\|^2\ge0\) and \((M-m)(\gamma^2-m-M)\|v\|^2\ge0\). These imply \(\gamma D+2m\mathcal E\le0\). Lean handles the equal-curvature case separately, expands the square in the strict case, and combines the scalar inequalities. Positive \(\gamma\) then permits division, giving \(D\le-2m\mathcal E/\gamma\).

steps.title: Obtain the sector condition from the actual potential
steps.body: For \(g=\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\) and displacement \(x-y\), the shared ULA library has already proved the strong-smooth interpolation inequality from differentiability, strong convexity and gradient Lipschitzness. potential_force_dissipativity applies that theorem, converts it to the sector condition, and feeds it into the completed-square estimate. Consequently no Hessian, sector bound, or contraction conclusion is assumed in this potential theorem. The explicit hypotheses retain \(m\le M\), \(\gamma>0\), and \(\gamma^2\ge m+M\).

steps.title: Differentiate the noise-cancelled path energy
steps.body: Assume \(v'=-\gamma v-g\) and \(x'=v\). Then \((v+\gamma x)'=-g\), while \((-v)'=\gamma v+g\). Lean obtains these two derivative formulas by addition, negation and constant scalar multiplication, normalizes them with module, and applies the squared-norm derivative rule to each coordinate. Their sum is precisely forceEnergyDerivative. The theorem assumes differentiability of the difference paths; it does not incorrectly differentiate an individual Brownian velocity path.

steps.title: Integrate energy decay and take the position square root
steps.body: For two continuous position paths \(x,y\), set \(F(t)=\mathcal E(v_t,x_t-y_t)\). The derivative theorem and potential dissipativity give \(F'\le-2mF/\gamma\). Closed-interval continuity and the explicit derivative witnesses allow the same Gronwall theorem as in the spectral proof, giving \(F(t)\le F(0)e^{-2mt/\gamma}\). If \(v_0=0\), then \(F(0)=\gamma^2\|x_0-y_0\|^2\). Combine with the position projection bound, cancel the positive \(\gamma^2\), and compare nonnegative squares. The exponential square identity \((e^{-mt/\gamma})^2=e^{-2mt/\gamma}\) yields \(\|x_t-y_t\|\le\sqrt2e^{-mt/\gamma}\|x_0-y_0\|\). This is a proved nonlinear pathwise estimate with the paper's correct prefactor.

steps.title: Use right derivatives at the initial time
steps.body: A finite-horizon integral solution is constrained only for nonnegative time. Its extension to negative time need not have the same derivative. The correct initial derivative is therefore the derivative within the right half-line. The product and squared-norm derivative rules remain valid in this form, so differentiating the transformed energy gives the same force-energy expression. Lean applies those within-derivative rules to both transformed coordinates, cancels the opposing friction terms, and transfers the resulting derivative to the energy expression. The right-slope form of Gronwall requires exactly these hypotheses, and gives the same exponential energy decay throughout the closed interval. This is the version used by the actual integral-flow theorem.

KineticLangevin/Hessian.lean.title: Construct the actual averaged Hessian on a segment
KineticLangevin/Hessian.lean.summary: The mean Hessian is a Bochner integral of the continuous derivative of the force along the segment between two positions. The module derives its self-adjointness, lower and upper quadratic-form bounds and exact representation of the force difference. Thus the operator used in the spectral contraction proof is a concrete object, not an assumed matrix already chosen to make the desired equation hold.

steps.title: Define the segment average and commute it with a pairing
steps.body: Set \(\bar H(x,y)=\int_0^1H(y+t(x-y))dt\). Continuity of \(H\) makes the operator-valued integrand continuous and integrable on the compact segment. A continuous linear map commutes with a Bochner integral, so applying the operator to \(w\) and pairing with \(z\) gives \(\langle z,\bar H(x,y)w\rangle=\int_0^1\langle z,H(y+t(x-y))w\rangle dt\). Lean first commutes operator evaluation through the interval integral, then commutes the continuous linear inner-product functional. The operator type is complete because the underlying Hilbert space is complete.

steps.title: Average symmetry and both spectral inequalities
steps.body: If every \(H(p)\) is self-adjoint, the pairing identity moves both sides into scalar integrals, where their integrands agree pointwise. If \(m\|z\|^2\le\langle z,H(p)z\rangle\le M\|z\|^2\), integral monotonicity bounds the average between the integrals of these two constants. The interval has length one, leaving exactly the original constants. Lean supplies continuity and interval-integrability for each quadratic-form integrand and the constant comparison function, applies integral_mono_on, and simplifies the constant integral. These results provide the genuine symmetry and spectral premises needed by the transformed-energy proof.

steps.title: The fundamental theorem identifies the actual force difference
steps.body: Assume \(Dg(p)=H(p)\). The affine path \(\ell(t)=y+t(x-y)\) has derivative \(x-y\), so the chain rule gives \((g\circ\ell)'(t)=H(\ell(t))(x-y)\). Integrate this derivative from zero to one. The fundamental theorem yields \(\int_0^1H(\ell(t))(x-y)dt=g(x)-g(y)\). Commuting the operator evaluation with the average integral gives \(\bar H(x,y)(x-y)=g(x)-g(y)\). Lean constructs the affine-path derivative, composes the force derivative at each segment point, verifies integrability from continuity, and simplifies the endpoints. No coordinatewise mean-value theorem or unjustified single Hessian point is used.

KineticLangevin.lean.title: Kinetic proof library and imports
KineticLangevin.lean.summary: This root module imports the checked components of the kinetic development. Its dependencies contain the exact mathematical statements, assumptions and complete Lean proofs. An import collection does not by itself assert that every theorem in the source paper has been formalized; the source correspondence audit separately records the required full stochastic-law endpoints.

KineticLangevin/Check.lean.title: Logical-axiom audit
KineticLangevin/Check.lean.summary: This audit asks Lean to print the logical axioms used by selected declared results. It helps detect unproved assumptions masquerading as proofs. Passing an axiom audit checks the listed declarations; it does not establish source-paper completeness. The full required stochastic endpoints remain separately listed in the reference audit.

KineticLangevin/Recurrence.lean.title: The first-order scalar accumulation and its exact scope
KineticLangevin/Recurrence.lean.summary: The numerical accumulation part of the KLMC proof begins with an explicit one-step coupling inequality. This module derives the stable contraction coefficient and sums its affine recurrence, retaining the coupling inequality and reference velocity norm as visible hypotheses. It therefore checks the numerical implication without claiming the still-open Gibbs stationarity and actual Gaussian-chain Wasserstein endpoint.

steps.title: Prove the one-sided exponential quadratic estimate
steps.body: For \(x\ge0\), let \(F(x)=1-x+x^2/2-e^{-x}\). Its derivative is \(-1+x+e^{-x}\), nonnegative because \(e^{-x}\ge1-x\). Therefore \(F\) is nondecreasing and \(F(x)\ge F(0)=0\), proving \(e^{-x}\le1-x+x^2/2\). Lean constructs the derivative through the polynomial and exponential derivative rules, proves its sign with Real.add_one_le_exp, applies the derivative monotonicity criterion, and evaluates the zero endpoint. The estimate is proved analytically rather than introduced as an unchecked Taylor remainder.

steps.title: Keep most of the exact-flow contraction after the local correction
steps.body: Set \(r=m/\gamma\). Suppose \(r,M,h\ge0\), \(2r^2\le M\), and \(4Mh\le r\). The quadratic exponential estimate gives \(e^{-rh}+3Mh^2/4\le1-rh+r^2h^2/2+3Mh^2/4\). Since \(r^2/2\le M/4\), the positive correction is at most \(Mh^2\le rh/4\). Thus the total is at most \(1-3rh/4\). Lean multiplies the curvature and step inequalities by the nonnegative time powers and combines them with nlinarith. The next theorem derives both scalar conditions from \(m>0\), \(m\le M\), \(\gamma^2\ge m+M\) and \(4\gamma Mh\le m\), dividing only by positive \(\gamma\) or \(\gamma^2\).

steps.title: Sum the affine recurrence with the visible local-coupling premise
steps.body: Assume nonnegative errors satisfy \(e_{n+1}\le e^{-rh}e_n+3Mh^2(C+e_n)/4\), with \(r,h>0\), \(C\ge0\), and the scalar restrictions above. Put \(q=1-3rh/4\). The coefficient bound and positivity of the exponential prove \(0\le q<1\), and multiplying that bound by \(e_n\ge0\) yields \(e_{n+1}\le qe_n+3Mh^2C/4\). The shared affine-recurrence theorem gives \(e_n\le q^ne_0+(3Mh^2C/4)/(1-q)\). Positive \(r,h\) permit denominator cancellation, leaving \(e_n\le q^ne_0+MhC/r\). Lean uses field_simp and ring only for that final quotient. The one-step coupling inequality is an explicit assumption, so this result must not be presented as the full actual-law KLMC theorem.

steps.title: Restore the paper’s physical parameters and position coefficient
steps.body:
Substitute \(r=m/\gamma\) into the scalar recurrence theorem. The derived scalar conditions justify the call, and rational simplification gives \(e_n\le(1-3mh/(4\gamma))^ne_0+\gamma MhC/m\). Suppose in addition that \(d_n\le\sqrt2e_n/\gamma\) and \(e_0\le\gamma d_0\). The nonnegative projection factor and nonnegative power of the proved stable contraction coefficient allow multiplication of these inequalities. Canceling \(\gamma\) yields

\[d_n\le\sqrt2(1-3mh/(4\gamma))^nd_0+Mh\sqrt2C/m.\]

Lean explicitly proves the projection factor and contraction coefficient nonnegative before transporting inequalities, then uses field_simp for the scalar cancellations. Setting \(C=\sqrt p\) matches the paper’s numerical expression. The local coupling, projection and initialization bounds remain explicit hypotheses on sequences; neither declaration identifies \(d_n\) with actual Wasserstein error or constructs a stationary reference.

KineticLangevin/Thermostat.lean.title: Exact Gaussian invariance of the velocity thermostat
KineticLangevin/Thermostat.lean.summary: The O substep removes velocity variance through damping and restores exactly that variance through independent Gaussian noise. This module proves an equality of probability measures, not only a matching second moment. Invariance of this substep is one component of kinetic stationarity; the Hamiltonian evolution and the full diffusion require separate arguments.

steps.title: Independent Gaussian linear combinations
steps.body:
Let \(G,G\prime\) be independent standard Gaussian vectors in a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space, and suppose \(a^2+b^2=1\). For a continuous linear functional \(L\), the characteristic function of \(aG+bG\prime\) is

\[\exp(-a^2\|L\|^2/2)\exp(-b^2\|L\|^2/2)=\exp(-\|L\|^2/2).\]

Independence is represented by the product of two standard Gaussian measures. Lean constructs the continuous linear map \(A(v,w)=av+bw\), uses charFunDual_map to pull the test functional back through \(A\), and uses charFunDual_prod to factor its characteristic function. The restrictions of \(L\circ A\) to the two factors are \(aL\) and \(bL\), proved by extensionality. The norm of a scalar multiple supplies the squared coefficients. The relation \(a^2+b^2=1\) then simplifies the exponent, and uniqueness of characteristic functions proves the distributional identity.

steps.title: Apply the fluctuation-dissipation balance
steps.body: For nonnegative friction and time step, put \(\delta=e^{-\gamma h/2}\) and \(s=\sqrt{1-\delta^2}\). The variance under the square root is nonnegative, so \(s^2=1-\delta^2\). Hence \(\delta^2+s^2=1\), and the preceding theorem gives \(\delta G+sG\prime\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\). Lean applies the general linear-combination theorem, rewrites the square root squared using its proved nonnegativity, unfolds the variance, and finishes with a polynomial identity. This is precisely the standard-temperature O half-step used in OBABO.

KineticLangevin/IntegralCoupling.lean.title: Shared-noise cancellation and uniqueness of the actual integral solution
KineticLangevin/IntegralCoupling.lean.summary: Individual kinetic velocity paths contain continuous noise and need not be differentiable. Their difference under the same additive forcing is differentiable from the right, because the forcing cancels in the integral equations themselves. This module derives that assertion and proves uniqueness by Gronwall, including the initial time.

steps.title: Subtract the two integral equations
steps.body:
Suppose \(Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^t g(Y_s)ds+B_t\) and \(Z_t-Z_0=-\int_0^t g(Z_s)ds+B_t\), with continuous paths and a Lipschitz drift. Subtraction gives

\[Y_t-Z_t=Y_0-Z_0-\int_0^t[g(Y_s)-g(Z_s)]ds.\]

The two drift integrals exist on every compact interval because their integrands are continuous. Lean first establishes interval integrability, distributes the difference through the integral, rewrites both supplied equations as expressions for the paths, and cancels the common forcing with the additive-group tactic. No derivative of the noise is taken.

steps.title: Differentiate after cancellation, including the initial endpoint
steps.body: The integrand \(g(Y_s)-g(Z_s)\) is continuous. The fundamental theorem of calculus therefore differentiates the integral expression, producing the right derivative \(-(g(Y_t)-g(Z_t))\). The identity is known only for \(t\in[0,T]\); consequently the mathematically appropriate conclusion at zero is a derivative within \([t,\infty)\). Lean builds an eventual neighborhood lying inside the valid time interval and transfers the derivative from the integral formula using eventual equality. This avoids imposing an arbitrary differentiable extension of the stochastic path to negative time.

steps.title: Uniqueness from the global Lipschitz bound
steps.body: For \(D=Y-Z\), the derived derivative obeys \(\|D\prime_t\|\le L\|D_t\|\). Equal initial conditions give \(\|D_0\|=0\). Gronwall then yields \(\|D_t\|\le0\) throughout the finite horizon. Lean passes the right-derivative theorem to its norm version of Gronwall, simplifies the zero initial bound, and uses definiteness of the norm to recover \(Y_t=Z_t\). This result supplies uniqueness for any continuous additive forcing, including the forcing used in the kinetic Picard construction.

KineticLangevin/MildError.lean.title: Identify the implemented exponential-step error with its actual integral defect
KineticLangevin/MildError.lean.summary: The local errors are concrete integrals of changes in the force. This module proves that these integrals really are the errors of the implemented exponential step when compared with a mild exact velocity and its integrated position. The variation-of-constants equation is an explicit input here; constructing its Brownian convolution and deriving it from the original integral equation remain distinct steps.

steps.title: Separate the frozen force from its variation
steps.body:
Write \(D_v(t)=\int_0^t e^{-\gamma(t-s)}[g(x_s)-g(x_0)]ds\). Linearity and \(\int_0^t e^{-\gamma(t-s)}ds=\psi_1(t)\) give

\[D_v(t)=\int_0^t e^{-\gamma(t-s)}g(x_s)ds-\psi_1(t)g(x_0).\]

Lean proves interval integrability using continuity of the path, drift and exponential kernel; it then distributes scalar multiplication and the integral over subtraction. For a mild exact velocity \(V_t=\psi_0(t)V_0-\int_0^t e^{-\gamma(t-s)}g(x_s)ds+B_t\), subtracting it from the frozen velocity plus the same convolution \(B_t\) gives exactly \(D_v(t)\). The proof is algebra after the integral identity.

steps.title: Integrating the frozen velocity gives the position formula
steps.body: The frozen position is \(x+\psi_1(t)v-\psi_2(t)g\). Its derivative is the frozen velocity \(\psi_0(t)v-\psi_1(t)g\), and its value at zero is \(x\). The fundamental theorem of calculus gives \(\int_0^t V_{\rm frozen}(s)ds=X_{\rm frozen}(t)-x\). Lean invokes the already proved derivative theorem and proves integrability from continuity of the coefficients. The identity holds also at zero friction because the coefficients were defined by integrals.

steps.title: Both coordinates use the same noise convolution
steps.body:
The position innovation is \(\int_0^h B_sds\), the time integral of the same velocity convolution. If \(x_h-x_0=\int_0^hV_sds\), integrate the velocity error identity to obtain the position defect \(D_x(h)=\int_0^hD_v(s)ds\). Thus

\[\operatorname{exponentialStep}(V_0,x_0;B_h,\int_0^hB_sds)-(V_h,x_h)=(D_v(h),D_x(h)).\]

Lean proves the velocity identity at every point in the interval, changes the integrand using that pointwise equality, distributes the integral over sums and differences, and uses the frozen-velocity integral and the kinematic identity. Extensionality then joins the two coordinate equalities into the phase-space equality. No stochastic error estimate is hidden inside the definitions.

steps.title: Bound the implemented step in the transformed norm
steps.body: Apply the exact step-error identity to replace exponentialStep − exact endpoint by the explicit pair \((D_v,D_x)\). The local-error module has already integrated the kinematic velocity bound to prove \(\mathcal E(D_v,D_x)\le(3MC h^2/4)^2\) under \(\gamma h\le1/4\). The norm-square identity and nonnegativity allow transformNorm_le_of_energy_le to take square roots, giving \(\|\text{step}-\text{exact}\|_T\le3MC h^2/4\). Every input is visible: the actual mild velocity equation, continuous common convolution noise, the kinematic identity, and the uniform velocity norm bound. No stochastic moment or stationary law is asserted here.

KineticLangevin/SynchronousFlow.lean.title: Contraction of actual shared-input kinetic integral solutions
KineticLangevin/SynchronousFlow.lean.summary: This joins the Picard integral construction to the transformed-energy argument. Two actual solutions with the same continuous forcing have a noise-free difference equation as a consequence of their integral identities. The energy estimate and the paper's position decay then follow without assuming either a contraction result or a differentiable Brownian path.

steps.title: Derive the phase difference equation and contract its energy
steps.body:
Apply the shared-input derivative theorem to the concrete kinetic drift \(G(v,x)=(\gamma v+ abla f(x),-v)\). Project its right derivative to velocity and position using the two continuous linear projection maps. The velocity derivative becomes \(-\gamma(V-V\prime)-[ abla f(X)- abla f(X\prime)]\); the position derivative is \(V-V\prime\). Scalar multiplication and additive rearrangement justify both identities. The right-derivative energy theorem, which is valid at the initial endpoint, yields

\[\mathcal E_t\le e^{-2mt/\gamma}\mathcal E_0,\quad\mathcal E_t=\|V_t-V\prime_t+\gamma(X_t-X\prime_t)\|^2+\|V_t-V\prime_t\|^2.\]

In Lean the required Lipschitz constant for \(G\) is derived from the actual gradient bound; it is not an extra Hessian or solution assumption. The argument then supplies the original potential's strong convexity and smoothness hypotheses to the proved energy inequality.

steps.title: Equal initial velocities give the sharp position prefactor
steps.body: If the initial velocities agree, \(\mathcal E_0=\gamma^2\|X_0-X\prime_0\|^2\). The projection estimate \(\gamma^2\|X_t-X\prime_t\|^2\le2\mathcal E_t\) cancels the factor \(\gamma^2\), giving the squared position bound. Positivity of \(\gamma\), the norm, the exponential and the square root permits taking square roots. Lean explicitly proves \(e^{-mt/\gamma\,\cdot2}=(e^{-mt/\gamma})^2\), rewrites \((\sqrt2)^2=2\), and applies the nonnegative square comparison theorem. The resulting prefactor is \(\sqrt2\), consistent with the explicit general prefactor in the supplied source.

steps.title: Contract the full transformed norm
steps.body: The actual integral-flow energy theorem gives \(\mathcal E_t\le e^{-2mt/\gamma}\mathcal E_0\). Replacing energy by the square of transformNorm and using \((e^{-mt/\gamma})^2=e^{-2mt/\gamma}\) gives \(\|Y_t-Z_t\|_T\le e^{-mt/\gamma}\|Y_0-Z_0\|_T\). Lean proves the exponential square identity by Real.exp_add, notes that both norms and the exponential are nonnegative, and invokes the energy-to-norm lemma. This stronger phase estimate controls velocity differences and accumulates discretization errors without a separate projection loss at each step.

steps.title: Apply the full shifted theorem to actual integral flows
steps.body:
Take two actual kinetic integral solutions with the same additive input. Their noise-cancelled phase difference has a right derivative by integral_difference_hasDerivWithinAt. Compose this derivative with the continuous linear velocity and position projections; module normalizes their drift formulas. The centered-sector theorem then supplies the full arbitrary-shift energy exponent from the original potential assumptions. Equal initial velocities identify the exact initial energy, and the position-square projection supplies the final prefactor. Squaring the desired nonnegative quantities, using the exponential-addition identity, and dividing by \(\gamma-2a>0\) proves

\[\|X_t-Y_t\|\le\frac{\sqrt{2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)}}{\gamma-2a}\exp\!\left(\frac{\max\{a^2-m,M-(\gamma-a)^2\}}{\gamma-2a}t\right)\|X_0-Y_0\|.\]

No continuous-Hessian assumption or difference-ODE assumption remains; both the ODE and the coefficient are derived from the concrete integral paths.

KineticLangevin/Flow.lean.title: The actual kinetic solution depends continuously on its initial state and noise path
KineticLangevin/Flow.lean.summary: Picard existence alone does not ensure a selected solution can be used as a measurable random process. This module proves stability when both the initial condition and continuous forcing vary, then constructs the actual kinetic flow by selection from the existing existence theorem. The stability estimate proves that the selected endpoint, and indeed the whole compact solution path, is jointly Lipschitz. No measurability, output-law identity or contraction conclusion is postulated.

steps.title: Subtract the rough forcing before differentiating
steps.body: Let \(Y_t-x=-\int_0^tg(Y_s)ds+B_t\) and \(Z_t-y=-\int_0^tg(Z_s)ds+C_t\). The inputs \(B,C\) are continuous and may be nowhere differentiable. Set \(F_t=Y_t-Z_t-(B_t-C_t)\). Subtract the integral equations to obtain \(F_t=x-y-\int_0^t(g(Y_s)-g(Z_s))ds\). This expression is differentiable from the right, including at the initial endpoint. If \(\|B_t-C_t\|\le D\), then \(\|Y_t-Z_t\|\le\|F_t\|+D\), and an \(L\)-Lipschitz drift gives \(\|F'_t\|\le(L+1)\|F_t\|+(L+1)D\). Gronwall and the initial equality \(F_0=x-y\) yield \(\|Y_t-Z_t\|\le(\|x-y\|+D)e^{(L+1)t}\). Lean proves equality with the differentiable integral expression on a right neighborhood and uses the within-derivative Gronwall theorem. The harmless extra one makes the coefficient strictly positive and avoids a special zero-Lipschitz case.

steps.title: Use compact paths with a uniform norm
steps.body: VelocityForcing T is the Banach space of continuous velocity-forcing paths on \([0,T]\), equipped with the supremum norm. The extension \(\widehat B_t=B(\operatorname{clip}_{[0,T]}t)-B(0)\) is continuous on the whole real line and starts at zero. This permits direct use of the proved finite-horizon Picard construction. Two normalized extensions satisfy \(\|\widehat B_t-\widehat C_t\|\le2\|B-C\|_\infty\): each of the two evaluation differences is bounded by the uniform norm. Lean uses continuity of the interval projection, evaluates at zero, and applies the norm triangle inequality to the two differences. No derivative of a forcing path is taken.

steps.title: Select an actual solution from proved existence
steps.body:
kineticFlow uses classical choice on exists_kinetic_integral, supplying the normalized forcing \((\widehat B_t,0)\). Its specification theorem retains all conclusions of that construction: the path is globally continuous, its initial phase is exactly the supplied phase, and it satisfies the concrete kinetic integral equation at every time on the horizon. Classical selection is justified because existence was proved analytically. It does not add a solution axiom. Subsequent stability between any two solutions makes every selected representative agree on the horizon and provides continuous parameter dependence.

kineticFlow_eq_of_integral applies the proved Lipschitz integral-equation uniqueness theorem to identify the selection with any other continuous solution driven by the same normalized forcing and initial phase. Thus a concrete Brownian realization can be identified with this canonical flow without assuming equality of endpoint laws.

steps.title: Prove joint endpoint continuity quantitatively
steps.body:
The kinetic negative drift has Lipschitz constant \(K_0=\gamma+uL+1\) in the product maximum norm. Apply the two-input estimate with forcing difference \(D=2\|B-C\|_\infty\). This gives

\[\|Y_t^{z,B}-Y_t^{w,C}\|\le(\|z-w\|+2\|B-C\|_\infty)e^{(K_0+1)t}.\]

In the product parameter norm both input differences are bounded by the same distance, so the endpoint is Lipschitz with constant \(3e^{(K_0+1)t}\). Lean derives the estimate from the actual selected paths and their specifications, then bounds each coordinate by the product norm. kineticFlow_endpoint_continuous follows from the Lipschitz theorem. Thus the eventual random endpoint map is measurable for a proved reason, even though its original existence definition used classical choice.

steps.title: Control the entire solution as a compact continuous path
steps.body: kineticFlowPath restricts the selected solution to \([0,T]\), retaining its proved continuity. At each time its difference has the endpoint bound. Since \(K_0+1\ge0\), \(e^{(K_0+1)t}\le e^{(K_0+1)T}\) on the horizon. The supremum-norm characterization then bounds the whole path difference by \(3e^{(K_0+1)T}\) times the initial-state/forcing-path distance. Lean applies ContinuousMap.norm_le, proves the pointwise exponential comparison, and uses the endpoint Lipschitz estimate. The resulting path-valued Lipschitz and continuity theorems support pushforwards into a genuine space of continuous trajectories, not merely separate endpoint choices.

KineticLangevin/FlowLaw.lean.title: Actual independent-source kinetic laws and their Wasserstein infimum
KineticLangevin/FlowLaw.lean.summary: The position law is an explicit pushforward of an independent product of the initial position law and a fixed source law for common initial velocity and continuous forcing. Every initial coupling is extended by that same source. The proof computes the two output marginals, preserves the initial cost, derives a coupling estimate and takes the infimum. The kinetic pointwise contraction is separately proved from the actual integral equation and the potential hypotheses; it is not an assumed convergence field.

steps.title: Define the independent random-map law and compute both output marginals
steps.body: For a measurable endpoint \(F(x,s)\), set \(\mathcal T_Q\mu=F_\#(\mu\otimes Q)\). Given any coupling \(c\) of \(\mu, u\), extend it to \(c\otimes Q\). Projecting to \((y,s)\) produces \( u\otimes Q\), because the second marginal of \(c\) is \( u\). Pushing further by \(F\) therefore gives \(\mathcal T_Q u\). Lean proves this with the product-map identity, the coupling's marginal equality, and pushforward composition. The corresponding first marginal uses the existing initialExtension_map. Both output-law identities are derived from the concrete product construction and are independent of which coupling was chosen.

steps.title: Lift pathwise contraction through L² and take all initial couplings
steps.body: Suppose the actual endpoint obeys \(\|F(x,s)-F(y,s)\|\le q\|x-y\|\) for each common source. On \(c\otimes Q\), the two outputs form a measurable coupling of \(\mathcal T_Q\mu,\mathcal T_Q u\). Pointwise contraction passes to the extended L² norm. The initial difference depends only on \(c\), so its norm on the product is exactly the original coupling cost. Thus \(W_2(\mathcal T_Q\mu,\mathcal T_Q u)\le q\,\operatorname{cost}(c)\) for every \(c\). Lean then applies the infimum theorem, using the independent product \(\mu\otimes u\) as a witness that couplings exist. No optimal-coupling attainment and no supplied output-law independence are required.

steps.title: Retain probability and justify the real-valued distance
steps.body: A measurable pushforward of \(\mu\otimes Q\) has total mass one when both inputs are probability measures; randomMapLaw_probability records this. The primary distance bound lives in the extended nonnegative reals, so infinite distances are preserved. If the initial Wasserstein distance is finite, the finite coefficient \(q\) makes its upper bound finite, and monotonicity of ENNReal.toReal gives the real-valued estimate. Lean proves that finiteness before converting the inequality, then rewrites the real value of the product. This avoids accidentally converting an infinite output distance to zero.

steps.title: Make the concrete kinetic endpoint a measurable random map
steps.body: The compact forcing space receives its Borel measurable structure. The source \(s=(v,B)\) contains initial velocity and a continuous forcing path; the separate input is initial position \(x\). kineticPositionMap evaluates the actual selected flow at phase \((v,x)\) and takes its position coordinate. The coordinate rearrangement \((x,(v,B))\mapsto((v,x),B)\) is continuous. Composing it with the proved joint endpoint continuity and projecting position gives continuity, hence measurability, of the actual map. Independence of source and position is implemented later by the explicit product measure rather than encoded as an unspecified output-law premise.

steps.title: Derive pointwise contraction from actual integral solutions
steps.body: Take two values of the selected kinetic flow with phases \((v,x)\) and \((v,y)\) and the same forcing path. Their specification gives the actual integral equations and equal initial velocities. The proved integral-synchronous theorem cancels their common forcing, derives the right-derivative difference equation, and applies the nonlinear potential energy estimate. Under differentiability, \(m\)-strong convexity, \(M\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(\gamma^2\ge m+M\), this yields \(\|F_t(x,s)-F_t(y,s)\|\le\sqrt2e^{-mt/\gamma}\|x-y\|\). Lean obtains the integral premises by rewriting the flow's initial-value specification, then simplifies the initial position and velocity projections. No differential equation or contraction conclusion is assumed of the chosen flow.

steps.title: Conclude the actual law-to-law kinetic theorem
steps.body:
kineticPositionLaw is the explicit independent-product pushforward for this concrete endpoint. Its probability theorem follows from endpoint measurability. Substituting the derived coefficient \(q=\sqrt2e^{-mt/\gamma}\) in the general random-map transport theorem gives

\[W_2(\mu_t,\nu_t)\le\sqrt2e^{-mt/\gamma}W_2(\mu_0,\nu_0).\]

The source law may be any fixed probability law of initial velocity and continuous forcing, independent of initial position. The statement therefore applies to any such stochastic realization; a stationary Gibbs law is unnecessary for comparing two evolving laws. The extended-valued theorem retains infinite initial costs, and the real-valued theorem explicitly requires finite initial Wasserstein distance. The full all-friction spectral prefactor and a canonical Brownian-source identification are separate refinements beyond this simple-friction law theorem.

steps.title: The full shifted prefactor and exponent pass to actual output laws
steps.body:
The actual-integral general contraction theorem uses the centered gradient sector estimate, so it requires differentiability, strong convexity and a Lipschitz gradient without adding Hessian continuity. For \(d=\gamma-2a>0\), its coefficient is

\[q_a(t)=\frac{\sqrt{2((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)}}{\gamma-2a} \exp\!\left(\frac{\max\{a^2-m,M-(\gamma-a)^2\}}{\gamma-2a}t\right).\]

The proof instantiates that actual-integral theorem with the same two selected flows and their proved specifications. The coefficient is nonnegative, so it can be bundled as an \(\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) scalar in the already proved random-map transport theorem. This yields \(W_2(\mu_t,\nu_t)\le q_a(t)W_2(\mu_0,\nu_0)\), with the genuine coupling infimum and internally derived output marginals. The real-valued version uses the same finite-initial-cost conversion. The theorem holds for every independent continuous-forcing source law; tying a constructed Brownian source and its required independence to the paper’s named diffusion remains separate, and no Gibbs invariant law is assumed.

KineticLangevin/BrownianConvolution.lean.title: Construct the correlated innovations from the same Brownian source
KineticLangevin/BrownianConvolution.lean.summary: The exponential schemes use correlated Brownian integrals, for example \(\xi_v=\int_0^t e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\,dB_s\) and \(\xi_x=\int_0^t\psi_1(t-s)\,dB_s\). Drawing two independent Gaussians would give the wrong algorithm. This module constructs these random variables on the explicit Gaussian probability space already used for the canonical Brownian motion. Their joint Gaussian law, all covariances, and continuity in L² are proved from the deterministic time kernels. The construction uses the existing isonormal isometry, which is the deterministic-kernel Wiener integral, rather than adding a hypothesis asserting that an unspecified noise has the required law.

steps.title: Reuse the existing Brownian probability space
steps.body: The time Hilbert space is \(H=L^2(\mathbb R,ds)\). The existing canonical Brownian construction selects a Hilbert basis of this space and places independent standard Gaussian coordinates on an explicit product probability space. Its isonormal map \(I:H\to L^2(\Omega,\mathbb P)\) is linear and preserves inner products. Brownian motion is represented there by \(B_t=I(1_{(0,t]})\). The three abbreviations reuse exactly this Hilbert space, sample space, and probability measure. No second independent Brownian source is introduced.

steps.title: Turn a continuous response into a genuine L² time kernel
steps.body:
For a continuous scalar response \(k\), define \(K_{k,t}(s)=1_{(0,t]}(s)k(t-s)\). The time reversal is essential: a Brownian fluctuation arriving at time \(s\) has \(t-s\) units of damping before the endpoint. Continuity of \(k\) gives a finite bound on the compact interval \([0,t]\). Since \((0,t]\) has finite Lebesgue measure, this bound proves square integrability.

Lean first uses memLp_indicator_iff_restrict to work on the finite interval measure. IsCompact.exists_bound_of_continuousOn provides an actual bound, and MemLp.of_bound proves membership in L². timeKernelLp then uses MemLp.toLp to form the equivalence class. Its selected representative agrees almost everywhere with the explicit indicator function, recorded by timeKernelLp_coe. Subsequent pointwise calculations therefore apply to the actual L² object.
