steps.title: Compute the time-kernel inner product exactly
steps.body:
The fundamental identity is

\[\langle K_{k,t},K_{\ell,t}\rangle_H=\int_0^t k(s)\ell(s)\,ds.\]

Start with the definition of the L² inner product as an integral. Replace both chosen representatives using their almost-everywhere formulas. Their product is zero outside \((0,t]\), and inside it equals \(k(t-s)\ell(t-s)\). Integrating the indicator restricts the integral to that interval. The substitution \(u=t-s\) reverses the endpoints and gives the displayed expression. Lean implements exactly these steps with L2.inner_def, integral_congr_ae, integral_indicator, and intervalIntegral.integral_comp_sub_left. This identity is the source of the covariance matrix, including its off-diagonal entries.

steps.title: Prove time continuity in L², including the moving endpoint
steps.body:
A moving indicator has a discontinuity at its endpoint, so pointwise continuity at every time coordinate is unavailable. Fix an endpoint \(t\). For every \(r\ne t\), the membership of \(r\) in \((0,s]\) is constant for all \(s\) sufficiently close to \(t\). If \(r<t\), ordinary continuity of \(k(s-r)\) applies; if \(r>t\), the kernel stays zero. The single exceptional time coordinate has Lebesgue measure zero.

The exact norm formula is

\[\|K_{k,s}-K_{k,t}\|_H^2=\int_{\mathbb R}|K_{k,s}(r)-K_{k,t}(r)|^2\,dr.\]

For \(s\) near \(t\), both kernels are supported in the fixed finite interval \((0,t+1]\). Compactness gives a common bound \(C\) for their values. The squared difference is therefore bounded by the integrable function \(4C^2 1_{(0,t+1]}\). Dominated convergence makes the squared L² distance tend to zero; continuity of the square root gives convergence of the distance itself.

Lean proves the pointwise limit by splitting the cases \(r<t\), \(r>t\), and \(r\le0\), with eventual inequalities supplied by the neighborhood filter. It obtains the norm formula from the L² inner product and the almost-everywhere subtraction formula. The continuity proof then applies tendsto_integral_filter_of_dominated_convergence, explicitly supplies the compact bound and the null singleton exception, and finishes with Real.continuous_sqrt. This proves continuity as an L²-valued map; it does not assert that the selected representatives have continuous sample paths.

steps.title: Apply the isonormal map and derive Gaussian moments
steps.body:
Define \(Z_k(t)=I(K_{k,t})\). This is the Wiener integral \(\int_0^t k(t-s)\,dB_s\) for a deterministic continuous kernel. The existing construction proves that every output of \(I\) is centered Gaussian and that \(\operatorname{Cov}(Iu,Iv)=\langle u,v\rangle_H\). Consequently,

\[\mathbb E Z_k(t)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(Z_k(t),Z_\ell(t))=\int_0^t k(s)\ell(s)\,ds.\]

The same linear map proves joint Gaussianity of every finite collection. This last statement is stronger than proving Gaussianity of each coordinate separately: all linear combinations must be Gaussian. Lean invokes the previously proved hasGaussianLaw_pi_of_linearMap_Lp, whose proof uses finite linear combinations and the linearity of the isonormal map. Covariance follows by rewriting the isonormal covariance theorem and the time-kernel inner-product identity. Time continuity follows by composing the continuous isometry with continuous_timeKernelLp.

steps.title: Identify the exact multivariate innovation law
steps.body:
For finitely many kernels \((k_i)\), assemble \(Z=(Z_{k_i}(t))_i\) as a Euclidean random vector. Its law is proved equal to \(\mathcal N(0,C)\), where \(C_{ij}=\int_0^t k_i(s)k_j(s)\,ds\). The conclusion compares the actual pushforward probability measure with kernelGaussian; equality of laws is not a premise.

Lean first transports the jointly Gaussian coordinate family through the continuous linear equivalence from a finite function space to Euclidean space. Coordinate L² membership gives vector L² membership, hence integrability. To identify the mean, the continuous coordinate projections commute with the Bochner integral and reduce every coordinate to the already proved zero mean. To identify covariance, covarianceBilin_apply_pi expands the covariance bilinear form as a finite double sum of coordinate covariances. The Brownian covariance identity turns that double sum into the matrix expression for the Gram covariance. IsGaussian.ext then concludes equality of the two Gaussian probability measures from equality of their means and covariance bilinear forms.

steps.title: Specialize to both kinetic schemes and check zero friction
steps.body:
The first-order velocity and position noises use \(k=\psi_0\) and \(k=\psi_1\), respectively. Their covariance is exactly klmcCovariance γ t 0 1, which generally is nonzero. The two-dimensional law theorem supplies the full first-order KLMC innovation, and the four-dimensional theorem uses \((\psi_0,\psi_1,\varphi_2,\varphi_3)\) to supply every correlated innovation needed by the Hessian-corrected second-order scheme. Both are direct specializations of the finite-family joint-law theorem, so each uses one common Brownian motion.

At zero friction, \(\psi_0\equiv1\), so the velocity convolution must reduce to the original Brownian variable \(B_t\). Lean verifies this as an equality in L²: the time kernel is precisely \(1_{(0,t]}\), the same indicator used in the canonical Brownian construction. The proof compares the actual almost-everywhere representatives with Lp.ext and indicatorConstLp_coeFn. The position and velocity L²-continuity statements follow from the general continuous-kernel theorem.

steps.title: Justify stochastic Fubini in the deterministic Hilbert space
steps.body:
The essential primitive identity is

\[K_{\psi_1,t}=\int_0^t K_{\psi_0,s}\,ds\quad\text{in }L^2(\mathbb R,dr).\]

Point evaluation on L² is not continuous, so one cannot simply evaluate a Bochner integral at a time coordinate and interchange the two integrals. The proof instead tests both sides against an arbitrary L² function \(f\). The inner product with a kernel is the ordinary integral \(\int_0^s f(r)e^{-\gamma(s-r)}\,dr\), a fact obtained from the actual almost-everywhere kernel representatives.

On the finite square \((0,t]^2\), consider \(1_{\{r\le s\}}e^{-\gamma(s-r)}f(r)\). For nonnegative friction the triangular exponential weight is bounded by one. The restriction of an L² function to a finite-measure interval is integrable, so the product is integrable on the square. This establishes the hypothesis of Fubini's theorem; the interchange is proved rather than assumed. After swapping, the inner integral is

\[\int_r^t e^{-\gamma(s-r)}\,ds=\psi_1(t-r).\]

Thus the two inner products agree for every \(f\), and Hilbert-space extensionality gives the vector identity.

Lean proves the two triangular-domain reductions by converting indicator integrals to restricted measures and explicitly identifying the intersections \((0,t]\cap(-\infty,s]=(0,s]\) and \((0,t]\cap[r,\infty)=[r,t]\). It removes the endpoint distinction using the null singleton property of Lebesgue measure. Integrable.comp_snd and Integrable.bdd_mul establish product integrability. integral_integral_swap applies Fubini, and ext_inner_left finishes after commuting the continuous inner-product functional with the Bochner integral.

steps.title: Obtain the actual kinetic Brownian integral equation
steps.body:
The scalar coefficient identity \(\psi_0(u)+\gamma\psi_1(u)=1\) holds pointwise, including at zero friction. Multiplying it by the time indicator and applying linearity of the isonormal map gives the exact relation

\[V_t^{\mathrm{noise}}+\gamma X_t^{\mathrm{noise}}=B_t.\]

The deterministic Hilbert primitive identity just proved transfers through the continuous linear isonormal map. Consequently,

\[X_t^{\mathrm{noise}}=\int_0^tV_s^{\mathrm{noise}}\,ds,\qquad V_t^{\mathrm{noise}}=B_t-\gamma\int_0^tV_s^{\mathrm{noise}}\,ds.\]

These are equations for the actual L² random variables whose joint Gaussian innovation law has already been identified. They connect the numerical exponential-integrator noise to the same additive Brownian forcing used by the kinetic diffusion.

For the first identity Lean compares actual representatives of the sum and scalar multiple of the time kernels, then applies friction_mul_psi_one. For the primitive identity, ContinuousLinearMap.intervalIntegral_comp_comm transports the deterministic Bochner integral through the isonormal map; its integrability is supplied by the proved L² time continuity. Finally, ordinary vector-space rearrangement gives the damped Brownian integral equation. No matching-noise law or integral-solution equation is introduced as a premise.

steps.title: Derive the explicit Brownian convolution by an integrating factor
steps.body:
The proved primitive identity implies \(P'_t=V_t\) for positive time. Combined with \(V_t+\gamma P_t=B_t\), this is the ordinary L²-valued equation \(P'_t+\gamma P_t=B_t\), with \(P_0=0\). Its integrating factor gives

\[\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(e^{\gamma t}P_t\bigr)=e^{\gamma t}B_t,\qquad P_t=\int_0^t e^{-\gamma(t-s)}B_s\,ds.\]

Substitution into the exact Brownian balance then gives the integration-by-parts representation

\[V_t=B_t-\gamma\int_0^t e^{-\gamma(t-s)}B_s\,ds.\]

Thus the isonormal Wiener integral and the continuous additive-Brownian forcing formulation are proved equal as actual L² vectors.

Lean first differentiates the indefinite integral defining the primitive. On a neighborhood of a positive time, coercing through Real.toNNReal does not change the endpoint, so HasDerivAt.congr_of_eventuallyEq transfers the derivative to positionLp. The product rule differentiates the scalar exponential times the L² vector. The Brownian balance cancels the damping term. The fundamental theorem of calculus on \([0,t]\), requiring derivatives only in its interior, then integrates this derivative. Multiplication by \(e^{-\gamma t}\) cancels the integrating factor. Finally, scalar multiplication commutes with the interval integral, and the exponential addition law converts \(e^{-\gamma t}e^{\gamma s}\) into \(e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\). This proof uses no sample-path differentiability of Brownian motion.

KineticLangevin/GeneralContraction.lean.title: Arbitrary-friction contraction directly from the potential
KineticLangevin/GeneralContraction.lean.summary: The paper's full shifted contraction can be derived from differentiability, strong convexity and a Lipschitz gradient alone. This proof centers velocity at \(v+\gamma x/2\), uses the strong-smooth sector inequality, and completes a scalar square. It removes any need to assume that the Hessian is continuous when constructing a mean Hessian, while recovering the exact maximum of the two endpoint curvature exponents.

steps.title: Center the phase energy and its derivative
steps.body:
The concrete force-difference derivative is \(2\langle v+(\gamma-a)x,-av-F\rangle+2\langle-v-ax,(\gamma-a)v+F\rangle\). Put \(y=v+\gamma x/2\), \(d=\gamma-2a\), and \(c=((\gamma-a)^2+a^2)/2\). Expanding the inner products gives the two exact identities

\[\mathcal E=2\|y\|^2+\tfrac12d^2\|x\|^2,\qquad \mathcal E'=-\gamma\mathcal E+4\langle y,cx-F\rangle.\]

The Lean proof rewrites squared norms as self-inner-products, distributes inner products over sums, differences and scalar multiplication, uses symmetry, and finishes with ring. These identities expose a scalar residual rather than a matrix diagonalization.

steps.title: Bound the residual around an arbitrary scalar curvature
steps.body: Strong-smooth interpolation places \(F\) in the ball centered at \(\mu x\), where \(\mu=(m+M)/2\), with radius \(R\|x\|\), where \(R=(M-m)/2\). Decompose \(cx-F=(c-\mu)x-(F-\mu x)\). The triangle inequality gives \(\|cx-F\|\le(|c-\mu|+R)\|x\|\). The coefficient is exactly \(\max\{c-m,M-c\}\): Lean splits on \(c\ge\mu\), simplifies the absolute value and the corresponding maximum, and checks the remaining arithmetic. No gradient or Hessian operator is invented in this argument.

steps.title: Complete the centered square to obtain the exact exponent
steps.body: Let \(K=\max\{c-m,M-c\}\ge0\). Cauchy–Schwarz and the residual bound give \(\langle y,cx-F\rangle\le K\|y\|\|x\|\). The nonnegative square \((2\|y\|-d\|x\|)^2\) implies \(4d\|y\|\|x\|\le2\mathcal E\). Multiplying by \(K\) and inserting the exact energy-derivative identity yields \(d\mathcal E'\le(-\gamma d+2K)\mathcal E\). Finally \(K=\max\{a^2-m,M-(\gamma-a)^2\}+\gamma d/2\), so the \(\gamma d\) terms cancel. Lean records the multiplied identities explicitly before nlinarith, then divides by the positive \(d\). This proves the precise spectral differential estimate even in a friction regime with a positive growth exponent.

steps.title: Supply the sector inequality from the actual potential
steps.body: For \(x-y\) and \(F=\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\), the project's proved strong_smooth_gradient_interpolation gives the strong-smooth interpolation inequality from Differentiable, StrongConvexOn and LipschitzWith. Its centered-ball consequence is exactly the residual theorem's premise. The proof composes these already proved results, yielding arbitrary-shift dissipativity for the actual nonlinear gradient. It assumes neither a Hessian representation nor the desired contraction conclusion.

steps.title: Integrate the right-derivative inequality
steps.body: The two kinetic difference equations imply the transformed-coordinate right derivatives \(-av-F\) and \((\gamma-a)v+F\). Their squared-norm derivative rules add to generalForceEnergyDerivative. For paths on \([0,T]\), define their transformed energy \(E(t)\). Continuity follows from continuity of the paths, while the preceding nonlinear result gives \(E'(t)\le2kE(t)\), with \(k=\max\{a^2-m,M-(\gamma-a)^2\}/(\gamma-2a)\). The right-slope form of Grönwall then proves \(E(t)\le E(0)e^{2kt}\), including the initial endpoint. The hypotheses are the actual force-difference differential equations, not an exponential bound supplied by the caller.

KineticLangevin/OneStep.lean.title: The concrete first-order contraction-and-defect inequality
KineticLangevin/OneStep.lean.summary: This theorem inserts an auxiliary exact kinetic path between the actual exponential numerical step and an exact reference endpoint. Its proof combines the implemented update's local error with continuous-time contraction. The reference velocity norm bound is an explicit hypothesis; establishing it from a stationary kinetic Gibbs law remains a probabilistic obligation.

steps.title: Control the auxiliary exact velocity from the reference
steps.body:
Let \(A\) be the exact path starting at the numerical phase point and \(R\) the reference path, driven by the same additive input. Put \(e=\|A_0-R_0\|_T\). The actual integral-flow theorem gives \(\|A_s-R_s\|_T\le e^{-ms/\gamma}e\le e\), because \(m,s\ge0\). Velocity projection and the triangle inequality therefore give \(\|A_s^v\|\le\|A_s^v-R_s^v\|+\|R_s^v\|\le e+C\). Lean derives the exponential comparison from Real.exp_le_one_iff, multiplies it by the nonnegative initial norm, invokes velocity_le_transformNorm, and combines the explicit reference bound with norm_add_le.

The mild equation identifies the implemented update's error relative to \(A_h\). Applying its proved local-norm theorem with \(C+e\) yields \(\|\operatorname{step}(A_0)-A_h\|_T\le3Mh^2(C+e)/4\). Finally insert \(A_h\) with the transformed triangle inequality and use exact-flow contraction between \(A_h\) and \(R_h\). The resulting concrete inequality is

\[\|\operatorname{step}(A_0)-R_h\|_T\le e^{-mh/\gamma}e+\tfrac34Mh^2(C+e).\]

The update noise is exactly \((B(h),\int_0^hB(s)\,ds)\); the raw additive input and its velocity convolution are both visible. This proves the local hypothesis used by the scalar recurrence from actual paths and actual update algebra, while making the remaining velocity-moment and Brownian-source identifications explicit.

KineticLangevin/Hamiltonian.lean.title: Exact Hamiltonian energy and volume-preserving Verlet geometry
KineticLangevin/Hamiltonian.lean.summary: The Hamiltonian subflow is the kinetic equation with zero friction and zero noise. Its total energy is conserved by an exact cancellation between force work and kinetic-energy change. This module proves conservation for the actual Picard-constructed integral flow and proves that the explicit kick/drift/Verlet maps preserve product Haar volume. These are genuine prerequisites for Gibbs stationarity; energy conservation alone and volume preservation of a numerical map do not yet establish invariance of the full kinetic diffusion.

steps.title: Differentiate total energy along the actual Hamiltonian equations
steps.body: Define \(H(v,x)=f(x)+\|v\|^2/2\). If \(x'=v\) and \(v'=- abla f(x)\), the chain rule gives \((f(x))'=\langle abla f(x),v angle\), while the squared-norm derivative gives \((\|v\|^2/2)'=-\langle v, abla f(x) angle\). Symmetry of the real inner product makes their sum zero. Lean composes the actual Fréchet derivative of \(f\) with the position derivative, uses the gradient representation of that derivative, and combines it with the Hilbert squared-norm derivative. The statement uses right derivatives within \([t,\infty)\), allowing the initial endpoint of an integral solution.

steps.title: Turn vanishing right derivatives into exact conservation
steps.body: A continuous scalar function with zero right derivative on \([0,T)\) is constant on \([0,T]\), including the final endpoint. The proof applies the scalar Gronwall comparison with coefficient and forcing both zero, first to \(F\) and then to \(-F\). These give \(F(t)\le F(0)\) and \(-F(t)\le-F(0)\). Their combination proves equality. This avoids assuming a derivative of the chosen extension beyond the terminal time or on negative time.

steps.title: Conserve energy for the constructed Hamiltonian integral flow
steps.body: hamiltonianFlow is the already constructed kineticFlow with friction zero, inverse mass one, and the zero compact forcing path. Its specification reduces to \(Y_t=Y_0-\int_0^tD(Y_s)ds\), with \(D(v,x)=(\nabla f(x),-v)\). Continuity of the Lipschitz drift gives the integral derivative. Lean identifies the selected path with its differentiable primitive on a right neighborhood, projects its derivative onto velocity and position, and applies the energy derivative cancellation. The scalar constancy theorem then yields \(H(Y_t)=H(Y_0)\). This is an exact statement about an existing solution, not an energy-preservation hypothesis on an abstract flow.

steps.title: Build the reversible proposal and preserve the Hamiltonian under reversal
steps.body: Velocity reversal \(R(v,x)=(-v,x)\) conjugates every kick and drift to its negative-time inverse. Applying this to the palindromic kick–drift–kick composition gives \(R\,V_h\,R=V_{-h}\). Since \(V_{-h}V_h=\mathrm{id}\), the proposal \(J_h=R\,V_h\) satisfies \(J_h^2=\mathrm{id}\). Lean rewrites the three component conjugacies and then uses the proved inverse Verlet identity. Negating velocity leaves its squared norm unchanged, so \(H(Rz)=H(z)\). The exact involution will give symmetric old/new proposal graph measures in the Metropolis argument.

steps.title: Expose the exact numerical energy defect
steps.body:
Let \(w=v-hg(x)/2\), \(y=x+hw\), and \(v^+=w-hg(y)/2\). Expanding both kinetic-energy squares gives

\[H(v^+,y)-H(v,x)=f(y)-f(x)-\frac h2\langle w,g(x)+g(y)\rangle +\frac{h^2}{8}\bigl(\|g(y)\|^2-\|g(x)\|^2\bigr).\]

The first part is a trapezoidal force-work remainder. The second is an explicit force-norm correction. Lean first proves the two-half-kick norm identity for arbitrary vectors using squared-norm and inner-product expansions, then substitutes the actual intermediate Verlet velocity and position. This identity preserves the error terms that must later be bounded to control rejection; no second-order error estimate is assumed by definition.

steps.title: Prove the elementary subflows preserve Haar volume
steps.body: A drift \((v,x)\mapsto(v,x+hv)\) is a skew product whose second component is a translation for each fixed velocity. Translation invariance of Haar measure therefore proves preservation of the product measure. A kick \((v,x)\mapsto(v-hg(x),x)\) is the same construction after swapping the two phase coordinates; measurability of \(g\) suffices. Lean applies the measure-preserving skew-product theorem to translations, then conjugates the kick by the measure-preserving swap. Composition proves the complete Verlet map preserves product Haar volume. This derives the Jacobian-one property without presupposing differentiability of the force.

steps.title: The reversed Verlet proposal is a measure-preserving involution
steps.body: For a Haar factor also invariant under negation, velocity reversal preserves product measure: apply the negation-preserving map in the velocity coordinate and identity in the position coordinate. Composing this with the proved volume-preserving Verlet map gives volume preservation of the explicit proposal \(J_h\). Together with \(J_h^2=\mathrm{id}\), this supplies the two exact properties used by deterministic Metropolis detailed balance. Neither property asserts that the uncorrected finite-step Verlet map itself preserves the Gibbs weight.

KineticLangevin/HamiltonianMetropolis.le.title: Exact Gibbs invariance of an explicit corrected Verlet proposal
KineticLangevin/HamiltonianMetropolis.le.summary: A volume-preserving involution has a symmetric old/new-state graph measure. Weighting that graph by a positive target density and applying the ordinary Metropolis ratio makes its accepted flow symmetric. The rejected mass stays at the old state. This module proves exact invariance for the explicit reversed-Verlet proposal. Passing from these corrected proposals to the unadjusted Hamiltonian flow and then to the full kinetic diffusion still requires quantitative limits.

steps.title: Construct the proposal graph and derive its swap symmetry
steps.body: For \(J^2=\mathrm{id}\), the graph map is \(G(z)=(z,Jz)\). Swapping the old and new state gives \(\operatorname{swap}\circ G=G\circ J\). If \(J\) preserves a base measure \(\lambda\), pushforward composition yields \(\operatorname{swap}_\#G_\#\lambda=G_\#J_\#\lambda=G_\#\lambda\). Lean proves the pointwise graph identity using the involution equation, verifies graph measurability, and rewrites the two pushforward compositions. Thus symmetry of the graph measure is derived from the actual proposal rather than introduced as a detailed-balance field.

steps.title: Apply the accepted-flow argument to an arbitrary positive density
steps.body: Let the target be \(w\lambda\), with measurable \(w>0\). Its proposal joint law is \(G_\#(w\lambda)\). The pushforward-with-density theorem expresses this as the symmetric base graph weighted by \(w\) at its first coordinate. The Metropolis ratio is \(\min\{1,w(y)/w(x)\}\), so accepted joint density is \(\min\{w(x),w(y)\}\), symmetric under swapping. The checked shared Metropolis theorem proves that accepted new-state mass plus rejected old-state mass has the initial marginal. Lean computes that marginal by projecting the graph back to its first coordinate, giving the exact identity with \(w\lambda\). No invariant measure or acceptance-balance conclusion is assumed.

steps.title: Bound rejection by an actual energy increase
steps.body: For energy increment \(d\), rejection is \(1-\min\{1,e^{-d}\}\). If \(d\le0\), the proposed energy decreases and rejection is zero. If \(d\ge0\), the exponential tangent inequality \(e^{-d}\ge1-d\) gives rejection at most \(d\). Thus rejection is at most \(\max\{d,0\}\le|d|\). Lean splits the sign cases, rewrites the minimum and maximum with the corresponding exponential bounds, and applies the tangent inequality. This is a scalar probability bound; converting it to an L² trajectory error also requires the size of the rejected jump and must not silently assume that jump is of order \(h\).

steps.title: Instantiate the exact corrected Verlet Gibbs theorem
steps.body: Take \(\lambda\) to be product Haar phase measure, \(J_h=R\,V_h\) to be the constructed reversed Verlet proposal, and \(w(z)=e^{-H(z)}\). The Hamiltonian module proves that \(J_h\) is both an involution and measure preserving. Measurability of the potential and gradient proves measurability of the weight and proposal, and the exponential weight is strictly positive. The generic theorem therefore proves exact preservation of the actual Gibbs weighted measure by this Metropolis step. Its accepted state is velocity-reversed Verlet and its rejected state is the old state. Applying a further velocity reversal changes those to ordinary Verlet on acceptance and a velocity flip on rejection; any limiting kinetic argument must account for this distinction explicitly.

KineticLangevin/LpContraction.lean.title: The actual nonlinear kinetic coupling in L²
KineticLangevin/LpContraction.lean.summary: Random vectors form a Hilbert space under the L² norm. The gradient acts on these vectors through the project's pointwise lpDrift construction. This module lifts the centered strong-smooth inequality to that actual vector field, then proves contraction of actual kinetic integral paths in L². It does not introduce a hypothetical differentiable potential on the infinite-dimensional space of random variables.

steps.title: Lift the centered gradient inequality pointwise
steps.body: For deterministic points, strong convexity and Lipschitz gradient imply \(\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)-\frac{m+M}{2}(x-y)\|\le\frac{M-m}{2}\|x-y\|\). The lifted gradient agrees almost everywhere with pointwise application of the original gradient. Lean collects the almost-everywhere identities for subtraction, scalar multiplication and lpDrift_coe, rewrites the random-variable representatives, and applies the deterministic centered inequality at each sample. Lp.norm_le_mul_norm_of_ae_le_mul integrates this norm comparison, yielding the same constant in L². No independence or moment estimate beyond membership in L² is needed for this step.

steps.title: Derive the L² energy inequality from actual integral paths
steps.body: Two phase paths satisfy the concrete kinetic integral equations with the actual lifted gradient and common additive input. The noise cancels in those equations, so their difference has a right derivative. Continuous linear projections extract the velocity and position equations. The general centered dissipativity theorem applies in the Hilbert space L² because the preceding pointwise lift supplies its sector premise. Under \(\gamma^2\ge m+M\), the maximum curvature coefficient equals \(-m\), giving \(E'(t)\le-2mE(t)/\gamma\). Continuity and the right-slope Grönwall theorem prove \(E(t)\le E(0)e^{-2mt/\gamma}\). Taking nonnegative square roots, using the exponential-addition identity, gives the full transformed L² norm contraction.

KineticLangevin/LpOneStep.lean.title: Gaussian velocity moments and the stochastic local step
KineticLangevin/LpOneStep.lean.summary: This module proves the exact \(\sqrt p\) reference velocity norm from a standard Gaussian marginal, then combines the genuine L² nonlinear contraction with the actual exponential-integrator error. Its hypotheses display the Gaussian reference marginal and concrete exact integral paths; stationarity proving that marginal is a separate theorem.

steps.title: Obtain the exact velocity moment from its Gaussian law
steps.body: The standard Gaussian vector is the pushforward of independent scalar \(N(0,1)\) coordinates by WithLp.toLp 2. Compose that pushforward with coordinate evaluation; the finite-product marginal formula reduces its law to \(N(0,1)\), since every other coordinate measure has mass one. If an L² velocity random variable has this standard Gaussian vector law, composition of laws gives the scalar coordinate laws. The project's proved Gaussian-coordinate moment identity then yields \(\|V\|_{L^2}=\sqrt{\#\iota}\). Thus the reference moment is derived from the explicit distribution rather than supplied as a numerical norm assumption.

steps.title: Prove the concrete stochastic one-step inequality
steps.body:
Let \(A\) be the auxiliary exact L² path starting at the numerical phase point, and \(R\) a synchronously driven exact reference. Their transformed L² distance is at most its initial value \(e\), because \(e^{-ms/\gamma}\le1\) for nonnegative time. Velocity projection and the exact Gaussian reference moment therefore give \(\|A_s^v\|_{L^2}\le\sqrt p+e\). Apply the actual mild-equation local-error theorem with this velocity bound: the numerical exponential update differs from \(A_h\) by at most \(3Mh^2(\sqrt p+e)/4\). Insert \(A_h\) with the transformed Hilbert triangle inequality and contract its distance to \(R_h\). The result is \(e_{\mathrm{next}}\le e^{-mh/\gamma}e+\frac34Mh^2(\sqrt p+e)\). Because the ambient space is L², the Bochner-integral and Hilbert triangle estimates are precisely the stochastic Minkowski estimates required by the paper.

The proof is factored through a shared theorem with an explicit reference velocity radius \(C\ge0\). A uniform bound \(\|V_t^{\rm ref}\|_{L^2}\le C\) supplies \(C+e_k\) in the local defect and the terminal bias \(Mh\sqrt2C/m\). The standard-Gaussian statement is a thin specialization with the radius \(\sqrt p\) proved from its marginal law. This same shared theorem applies to particle temperature \(1/N\), using the separately proved thermal radius \(\sqrt{(d_\theta+Nd_x)/N}\); there is no duplicate exponential-integrator argument.

KineticLangevin/LpConvergence.lean.title: Iterating concrete stochastic segments to a Wasserstein bound
KineticLangevin/LpConvergence.lean.summary: The numerical phase knots, auxiliary exact segments, reference segments, common raw inputs and convolution noises are explicit. The local coupling inequality is proved internally from these paths. The remaining law inputs state the actual reference Gaussian velocity and stationary position marginals. They do not assume a convergence conclusion.

steps.title: Accumulate actual update errors and project to laws
steps.body:
For each step, the auxiliary path begins at the numerical knot, while the reference segment joins consecutive reference knots. The numerical knot update is exactly exponentialStep with innovation \((B(h),\int_0^hB(s)\,ds)\). Rewriting these endpoint identities in the proved L² one-step theorem produces the recurrence \(e_{k+1}\le e^{-mh/\gamma}e_k+3Mh^2(\sqrt p+e_k)/4\). The source step restriction \(4\gamma Mh\le m\), together with \(m\le M\), implies \(\gamma h\le1/4\), as needed for the local constant. The scalar recurrence theorem then gives \(e_n\le(1-3mh/(4\gamma))^ne_0+\gamma Mh\sqrt p/m\).

The actual numerical and reference position random variables provide a finite-cost Wasserstein coupling. The reference position law is the stated target \(\pi\), and position projection gives \(W_2\le\sqrt2e_n/\gamma\). Equal initial velocities identify \(e_0=\gamma\|X_0-Y_0\|_{L^2}\). Lean cancels friction and combines \(\sqrt2\sqrt p=\sqrt{2p}\), proving

\[W_2(\mathcal L(X_n),\pi)\le\sqrt2\left(1-\frac{3mh}{4\gamma}\right)^n\|X_0-Y_0\|_{L^2}+\frac{Mh\sqrt{2p}}m.\]

The initial term is the cost of the supplied coupling. Obtaining the infimum over all initial couplings, and discharging reference stationarity from the actual Brownian kinetic process, remain separate probabilistic requirements.

The proof is factored through a shared theorem with an explicit reference velocity radius \(C\ge0\). A uniform bound \(\|V_t^{\rm ref}\|_{L^2}\le C\) supplies \(C+e_k\) in the local defect and the terminal bias \(Mh\sqrt2C/m\). The standard-Gaussian statement is a thin specialization with the radius \(\sqrt p\) proved from its marginal law. This same shared theorem applies to particle temperature \(1/N\), using the separately proved thermal radius \(\sqrt{(d_\theta+Nd_x)/N}\); there is no duplicate exponential-integrator argument.

KineticLangevin/LpDynamics.lean.title: The L² recursion is the original implemented KLMC chain
KineticLangevin/LpDynamics.lean.summary: Analysis on equivalence classes of random vectors is useful only if it represents the intended algorithm. The lemmas here prove that the actual lifted exponential update, KLMC noise scaling and every recursively defined iterate agree almost everywhere with the original pointwise vector formulas. No Gaussian or independence assumptions are required for this algebraic correspondence.

steps.title: Read L² phase points and identify the exponential update
steps.body: lpPhaseCoe reads the velocity and position representatives of a pair of L² classes at the same sample. A private affine-operation lemma combines the almost-everywhere identities for scalar multiplication, subtraction and addition. Apply it to the velocity formula \(\psi_0v-\psi_1G(x)+\eta_v\). For position, rewrite its affine expression as \(\psi_1v-\psi_2G(x)+(x+\eta_x)\), then use the same lemma. Finally lpDrift_coe identifies \(G(x)(\omega)\) with \(\nabla f(x(\omega))\). The two component equalities give equality of the actual phase update and the original pointwise exponentialStep.

steps.title: Expand affine operations on L² representatives
steps.body: The representative of a sum or scalar multiple of Lp classes agrees with the corresponding operation almost everywhere. The private helper gathers the four rules needed for \(aX-bY+Z\) into one common full-measure set. On that set, it rewrites the representative of the outer sum, the inner difference, and the two scalar multiples. The resulting equality is precisely the pointwise affine formula. This step accounts for the fact that Lp elements are equivalence classes; pointwise equalities of their arbitrarily selected representatives cannot be assumed everywhere.

steps.title: Retain the exact KLMC noise scaling through every iterate
steps.body: The two phase components of a scaled L² innovation agree almost everywhere with the same scalar times their representatives. Combining this with the exponential-step correspondence proves the KLMC correspondence, including its \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\) fluctuation-dissipation factor. Induction then proves the entire chain identity: at zero both chains use the supplied initial point; at a successor, intersect the almost-everywhere previous-chain identity with the current-step identity, and rewrite the recursive definitions. This shows the L² error estimates concern the original numerical sampler for the supplied innovation stream, rather than a different abstract sequence.

KineticLangevin/Friction.lean.title: Optimizing friction and the shifted contraction exponent
KineticLangevin/Friction.lean.summary: The general kinetic theorem permits every shift \(0\le a<\gamma/2\). Its exponential coefficient is \(k(a)=\max\{a^2-m,M-(\gamma-a)^2\}/(\gamma-2a)\); a negative coefficient is a contraction rate. This module proves the three scalar optimization regimes in Table 1 of the supplied manuscript. It establishes both the value at the proposed shift and a lower bound valid for every admissible competing shift. Singular square-root and denominator boundaries are explicit. These are algebraic corollaries of the kinetic estimate, separate from construction of the Brownian process and its invariant law.

steps.title: Center the shift interval
steps.body:
Write \(d=\gamma-2a>0\). The two branches of the coefficient become

\[k(a)=-\frac\gamma2+\max\left\{\frac{d^2+\gamma^2-4m}{4d},\frac{4M-\gamma^2-d^2}{4d}\right\}.\]

The definition records the original coefficient exactly. For the centered identity, Lean proves each rational identity by expressing its numerator as \((-\gamma/2)d\) plus a quarter of the new numerator, distributing division, and cancelling the nonzero \(d\). Positivity allows the maximum to commute with division. Translating both branches by the same scalar then extracts \(-\gamma/2\). The denominator sign matters; a mere nonzero premise would not justify the maximum identity.

steps.title: Prove optimality of zero shift at low friction
steps.body: If \(\gamma^2\le m+M\) and \(m\le M\), the optimum is \(a=0\), with coefficient \((M-\gamma^2)/\gamma\). For any admissible \(a\ge0\), compare only the second branch to this value. After multiplying by the two positive denominators, their difference is \(a(2M-\gamma a)\), which is nonnegative under the regime assumptions. The full maximum is at least its second branch. Lean formalizes those two comparisons with the positive-denominator division lemmas and nlinarith. At zero, \(M-\gamma^2\ge-m\), so the maximum is exactly the second endpoint. In particular, \(\gamma^2\le M\) gives a nonnegative best exponent, explaining the table's absence of a contraction rate in that range.

steps.title: Balance the endpoints in the middle regime
steps.body:
Set \(D=\sqrt{2(m+M)-\gamma^2}\) and \(a=(\gamma-D)/2\). If \(\gamma^2\ge m+M\) and the radicand is strictly positive, then \(0<D\le\gamma\); hence the shift is admissible. Substituting \(D^2=2(m+M)-\gamma^2\) shows that the two curvature branches agree. The resulting coefficient is

\[k(a)=-\frac\gamma2+\frac{M-m}{2D}.\]

Lean proves the root sign and square first, establishes the denominator identity \(\gamma-2a=D\), rewrites the equal branches, and clears the positive denominator. It never evaluates the formula with \(D=0\).

steps.title: Check every competing shift at the middle corner
steps.body: Assume additionally \(\gamma^2\le3m+M\), and let \(d=\gamma-2a>0\) describe any competing shift. If \(d\le D\), compare the second branch with the balanced value. Clearing positive denominators factors its error as a positive multiple of \((D-d)(D^2+Dd+2(M-m))\). If \(d\ge D\), compare the first branch instead; the corresponding factor is \((d-D)(D(d-D)+2D^2-2(M-m))\). The last coefficient is nonnegative because \(\gamma^2\le3m+M\). Lean splits precisely on \(d\le D\), proves these products nonnegative, and uses the square identity for \(D\), also multiplied by \(D\), to close the polynomial comparisons. This proves global optimality, including the nondifferentiable corner of the maximum, without assuming a derivative there.

steps.title: Select the smaller characteristic root at high friction
steps.body:
For \(\gamma^2\ge3m+M\), let \(D=\sqrt{\gamma^2-4m}>0\) and \(a=(\gamma-D)/2\). Nonnegative \(m\) gives \(D\le\gamma\), so the shift is nonnegative and its coordinate denominator is \(D>0\). The identity \(a(\gamma-a)=m\) makes the first branch equal \(-a\), and the high-friction condition places the second branch below it. Therefore the rate is \(a=(\gamma-\sqrt{\gamma^2-4m})/2\).

For any competing shift, the first branch alone bounds the maximum from below. The inequality that it is at least \(-a\) is exactly the nonnegative square \((\gamma-2a'-D)^2\ge0\) after division by the positive competing denominator. Lean supplies that square to nlinarith, then uses the maximum comparison. The strict discriminant excludes the equal-curvature critical point where the selected transformation becomes singular; a separate limiting argument would be required at that point.

KineticLangevin/HamiltonianError.lean.title: Explicit Verlet energy and rejection estimates
KineticLangevin/HamiltonianError.lean.summary: The exact Hamiltonian defect proved earlier becomes quantitative under a globally Lipschitz gradient. The proof uses only first derivatives: two-sided Taylor control bounds the trapezoidal force work, while a norm factorization bounds the force-square correction. These estimates concern the actual algebraic Verlet map and can control the rejection mass of the invariant corrected approximation.

steps.title: Obtain the two-sided Taylor remainder
steps.body: The shared smooth upper bound gives \(f(y)-f(x)-\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\le M\|y-x\|^2/2\). Apply the same theorem to \(-f\). Its gradient is \(-\nabla f\), proved by rewriting the Fréchet derivative and the linear Riesz inverse, and its Lipschitz constant remains \(M\). The second application gives the reverse inequality, so the absolute remainder has the same bound. Lean explicitly rewrites the negative gradient and combines the upper and lower scalar inequalities with abs_le.

steps.title: Average Taylor errors from both endpoints
steps.body: Write \(d=y-x\), \(r_x=f(y)-f(x)-\langle abla f(x),d angle\), and \(r_y=f(x)-f(y)+\langle abla f(y),d angle\). The trapezoidal force-work error is exactly \((r_x-r_y)/2\). Both remainders have absolute value at most \(M\|d\|^2/2\). The triangle inequality therefore gives \[\left|f(y)-f(x)- frac12\langle abla f(x)+ abla f(y),d angle ight|\le frac M2\|d\|^2.\] Lean proves the algebraic average identity after expanding the inner product, reverses the displacement in the second Taylor bound, and applies the absolute-value triangle inequality.

steps.title: Control the squared-force correction
steps.body: Factor \(\|g(y)\|^2-\|g(x)\|^2=(\|g(y)\|-\|g(x)\|)(\|g(y)\|+\|g(x)\|)\). The reverse triangle inequality and Lipschitz continuity bound the first factor by \(M\|y-x\|\). The ordinary triangle inequality bounds the second by \(2\|g(x)\|+M\|y-x\|\). Multiplying these nonnegative estimates proves the displayed force-square bound. Lean derives the endpoint-force growth estimate before applying mul_le_mul, so every sign condition is checked.

steps.title: Bound the complete Verlet energy defect
steps.body: Set \(w=v-h abla f(x)/2\), \(y=x+hw\). The exact identity from the Hamiltonian module writes the defect as a trapezoidal work error plus \(h^2(\| abla f(y)\|^2-\| abla f(x)\|^2)/8\). Since \(\|y-x\|=|h|\|w\|\), the preceding two lemmas give \[|H(V_hz)-H(z)|\le rac M2h^2\|w\|^2+ rac{h^2}{8}M|h|\|w\| igl(2\| abla f(x)\|+M|h|\|w\| igr).\] Lean substitutes the actual intermediate stage, changes the inner product to the displacement form, applies the triangle inequality to the two exact defect terms, and simplifies \(|h|^2=h^2\). The leading term is quadratic in the step under only gradient Lipschitz regularity.

KineticLangevin/HamiltonianWeak.lean.title: The actual accepted-Verlet and rejected-flip invariant measure
KineticLangevin/HamiltonianWeak.lean.summary: The reversed-Verlet involution supplied exact Metropolis invariance. Applying one final velocity reversal gives ordinary Verlet on acceptance and a velocity flip on rejection. This module computes the resulting two weighted pushforward measures explicitly and proves that their sum equals the Hamiltonian Gibbs measure. This identity is the concrete starting point for bounded-test estimates and a numerical limit.

steps.title: Compute the two Metropolis graph marginals
steps.body: For a deterministic proposal \(J\), the old/new graph is \(G(z)=(z,Jz)\). Weighting its pushforward by a measurable acceptance function \(a(z,Jz)\) commutes with mapping the correspondingly weighted initial measure through \(G\). Projecting onto the second coordinate yields \(J_\#(a\pi)\). Projecting rejected mass onto the first coordinate yields \((1-a)\pi\). Lean applies the previously proved pushforward-with-density formula twice and composes each graph with its coordinate projection. This proves an actual equality of measures without an integrability premise.

steps.title: Construct the Hamiltonian Gibbs measure and prove velocity symmetry
steps.body: The measure is \(e^{-H(v,x)}(\mu\otimes\mu)(d(v,x))\), where \(\mu\) is a translation-invariant symmetric Haar factor and \(H(v,x)=f(x)+\|v\|^2/2\). It is initially unnormalized; finiteness and normalization are independent questions. Velocity reversal preserves product Haar measure and preserves \(H\) exactly. The weighted pushforward identity therefore proves that it preserves this Gibbs measure. Lean verifies measurability of the exponential density and rewrites the two exact preservation identities.

steps.title: Use the actual Verlet energy change as acceptance
steps.body: The acceptance probability is \(a_h(z)=\min\{1,\exp[-(H(V_hz)-H(z))]\}\). Its measurability follows by expanding the explicit kick-drift-kick stages and composing the measurable potential and gradient. Positivity of the exponential gives \(a_h\ge0\), and the minimum gives \(a_h\le1\). These scalar bounds later justify finite weighted measures and nonnegative rejection estimates.

steps.title: Derive exact corrected Verlet invariance
steps.body: The proved Metropolis result uses the involution \(J_h=R\circ V_h\). Since \(H\circ R=H\), its ratio is exactly the acceptance \(a_h\) just defined. Compute its accepted and rejected graph marginals, then push the resulting equality through \(R\). The accepted state becomes \(R(J_hz)=V_hz\), whereas the rejected state becomes \(Rz\). Gibbs velocity symmetry fixes the right-hand side, giving \[(V_h)_\#(a_h\pi)+R_\#((1-a_h)\pi)=\pi.\] Lean performs precisely these graph, density, and pushforward rewrites and uses the checked identity \(R^2=\mathrm{id}\). This theorem does not identify rejection with a small spatial jump; the rejected velocity flip is retained explicitly.

KineticLangevin/HamiltonianTests.lean.title: Bounded-test estimates from the exact corrected measure
KineticLangevin/HamiltonianTests.lean.summary: The rejected move can reverse a velocity of order one. A weak approximation therefore uses bounded complex-valued tests rather than assuming the rejected jump is proportional to the step. The exact corrected measure identity implies that one uncorrected proposal has test bias at most twice the test bound times its mean rejection probability.

steps.title: Keep all acceptance and rejection mass
steps.body: For measurable \(0\le a\le1\), the two weighted measures \(a\pi\) and \((1-a)\pi\) sum exactly to \(\pi\). Lean combines the two densities, uses nonnegativity to rewrite the sum of ENNReal.ofReal values as the value of their sum, and reduces the resulting density to one. In particular both weighted measures are bounded above by the original finite measure.

steps.title: Turn the explicit invariant measure into an integral identity
steps.body: Suppose the already constructed corrected measure satisfies \(V_\#(a\pi)+R_\#((1-a)\pi)=\pi\). This identity is proved for the actual Verlet and reversal maps in the preceding module. For bounded measurable complex \(F\), integration gives \[\int F\,d\pi=\int a(z)F(Vz)\,d\pi+\int(1-a(z))F(Rz)\,d\pi.\] Lean first proves finiteness of each weighted measure from the exact mass split. The bound on \(F\) supplies integrability for both pushforward measures. It then applies the Bochner integral formula for a pushforward and the formula for a density-weighted integral; the acceptance and rejection factors are finite nonnegative real numbers.

steps.title: Bound the entire rejected move through the test bound
steps.body: Subtract the invariant-test identity from the ordinary proposal expectation. The exact difference is \[\int F(Vz)\,d\pi-\int F\,d\pi=\int(1-a(z))\,[F(Vz)-F(Rz)]\,d\pi.\] If \(\|F\|\le C\), the norm of the bracket is at most \(2C\), irrespective of the size of the rejected physical jump. Since \(1-a\ge0\), the norm of the integral is at most \(2C\int(1-a)\,d\pi\). Lean explicitly checks bounded integrability of the proposal test, accepted test, rejected test, and rejection factor, rewrites the subtraction under the integral, applies the norm-of-integral inequality, and integrates the pointwise triangle bound. Thus the velocity flip is fully accounted for.

KineticLangevin/BrownianSegments.lean.title: Construct independent correlated innovations on Brownian time intervals
KineticLangevin/BrownianSegments.lean.summary: The one-step Gaussian covariance is only part of the algorithm: innovations at different iterations must be independent and must come from increments of the same Brownian source used by the exact reference. This module translates deterministic time kernels onto successive intervals of that source. Translation preserves the within-step Gram covariance. Disjoint time supports give zero cross covariances, and joint Gaussianity turns this orthogonality into independence of the entire innovation blocks. Correlations among coordinates within a block are retained.

steps.title: Translate a time kernel without changing its L² geometry
steps.body:
For an interval beginning at \(a\), translate the original response kernel by \((S_aK)(r)=K(r-a)\). Lebesgue measure is invariant under translation, so \(S_a\) is a real linear isometry of the deterministic time Hilbert space. The translated response is

\[K^{a,t}_k(r)=1_{(a,a+t]}(r)k(a+t-r).\]

Its inner product with another response on the same interval remains \(\int_0^t k(s)\ell(s)\,ds\).

Lean constructs the isometry with Lp.compMeasurePreservingₗᵢ and measurePreserving_sub_right. The representative theorem combines the almost-everywhere composition formula with the previously proved kernel representative. Elementary inequalities identify \(r-a\in(0,t]\) with \(r\in(a,a+t]\); scalar algebra identifies the two elapsed-time expressions. Inner-product preservation of the linear isometry then reduces the covariance geometry to the unshifted kernel identity.

steps.title: Prove that disjoint time segments are orthogonal
steps.body:
If \(a+t\le b\), the intervals \((a,a+t]\) and \((b,b+u]\) are disjoint. At every time coordinate, at least one of their indicators is zero. Their L² inner product is therefore zero, regardless of the two continuous response functions.

The Lean proof unfolds the L² inner product as an integral, substitutes the explicit almost-everywhere segment representatives, and splits on membership in the first interval. Membership implies \(r\le a+t\le b\), which excludes the strict lower bound \(b<r\) of the second interval. Thus the integrand vanishes almost everywhere, and integral_eq_zero_of_ae concludes. The half-open convention makes adjacent segments disjoint exactly, including their common endpoint.

steps.title: Apply the same isonormal map to every time segment
steps.body:
Define \(Z_k^{a,t}=I(K_k^{a,t})\) using the same isonormal map and Gaussian product sample space as the original Brownian motion. Each response is centered, and every finite family of responses on an interval is jointly Gaussian. The covariance on one interval is the same Gram integral as before. Responses on separated intervals have covariance zero by the deterministic support calculation.

Lean proves these assertions by composing the translation's linear map with the existing Gaussian isonormal map. The finite-family Gaussian theorem applies to that actual composite linear map. For covariances, isonormal_covariance reduces the probability calculation to the deterministic inner product, where the within-interval and disjoint-interval theorems apply. Independence is not assumed at this stage; zero covariance alone would not imply independence without the jointly Gaussian property proved next.

steps.title: Identify the full Gaussian block law on every interval
steps.body:
For finitely many response functions \((k_i)\), the Euclidean vector \((Z_{k_i}^{a,t})_i\) has exactly the centered Gaussian law with covariance \(C_{ij}=\int_0^t k_i(s)k_j(s)\,ds\). The starting time \(a\) does not appear in this law, because deterministic translation preserves all inner products.

Lean assembles the actual L² representatives into a Euclidean random vector and proves its Gaussianity via the continuous linear equivalence from finite function space. Coordinate projections commute with the Bochner integral, giving the zero vector mean. The covariance bilinear form expands into a finite double sum; each entry is rewritten by the proved segment covariance formula. Equality with the Gram Gaussian's bilinear form, together with equality of means, lets IsGaussian.ext identify the two probability measures. No distributional equality is supplied as a hypothesis.

steps.title: Derive independence of all successive Brownian innovation blocks
steps.body:
On the uniform grid, the \(n\)-th block uses the interval \((nh,(n+1)h]\). gridConvolutionLp places every response function on that interval. The family indexed by both iteration and response coordinate is a Gaussian process because every member is obtained by applying one Gaussian linear map to a deterministic Hilbert vector.

For \(n<m\), the elementary inequality \((n+1)h\le mh\) proves disjoint support and therefore zero cross covariance between every coordinate of the two blocks. The Gaussian-process independence theorem converts these coordinate covariance equalities into independence of the entire block-valued random variables, over all iteration numbers simultaneously. Packing a finite coordinate family into Euclidean space is a measurable map, so time independence survives that packing.

Lean constructs the jointly Gaussian process with isGaussianProcess_of_linearMap_Lp. It uses iIndepFun_of_covariance_eq_zero, proves the disjoint-segment inequality from Nat.succ_le_of_lt, and handles the reversed ordering through symmetry of covariance. Finally, iIndepFun.comp transports independence through WithLp.toLp. The per-block law is the segment joint-law theorem, so the actual Brownian-derived Euclidean blocks are identically distributed with the required correlated Gram-Gaussian law.

KineticLangevin/OBABOEnergy.lean.title: The OBABO metric and a rigorous nonlinear average-force estimate
KineticLangevin/OBABOEnergy.lean.summary: The OBABO source metric is \(E(v,x)=\|x\|^2+2\langle x,v\rangle/\gamma+\|v\|^2/L\). Its continuous drift is contractive when \(\gamma^2\ge4L\). OBABO evaluates the force at two different position pairs; the proof below controls their average by an explicit centered-sector error. This avoids selecting a single Hessian point in a vector-valued mean-value theorem. The higher-order discrete remainder still has to be bounded separately.

steps.title: Prove that the mixed energy defines the correct geometry
steps.body: Write \(E_{a,b}(v,x)=\|x\|^2+2b\langle x,v\rangle+a\|v\|^2\), and let \(E_{a,0}\) be its diagonal part. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the mixed inner product in both directions. The nonnegative square \((\|x\|-2b\|v\|)^2\), together with \(4b^2\le a\), gives \(|2b\langle x,v\rangle|\le E_{a,0}/2\). Lean records the two scalar inner-product comparisons, multiplies them by nonnegative \(2b\), and combines them with the squared difference using nlinarith. Thus \(E_{a,0}/2\le E_{a,b}\le3E_{a,0}/2\), and energy is nonnegative. For \(a=1/L,b=1/\gamma\), the positive-denominator division rules show that the coefficient condition is exactly \(\gamma^2\ge4L\).

steps.title: Derive the source drift with an explicit sector error
steps.body:
Along \(x'=v,v'=-\gamma v-F\), the energy derivative has common-denominator numerator \(-2L\langle x,F\rangle+(2L-2\gamma^2)\|v\|^2-2\gamma\langle v,F\rangle\). Suppose the force obeys \(\langle x,F\rangle\ge m\|x\|^2-e\|x\|\) and \(\|F\|^2\le L\langle x,F\rangle+Le\|x\|+e^2\). The nonnegative square \(\|\gamma v+F\|^2\) controls the velocity-force mixed term. Insert these inequalities, use the metric's upper equivalence, and use \(\gamma^2\ge4L\), \(0\le m\le L\) to discard the remaining nonpositive velocity term. Clearing the positive denominator \(\gamma L\) proves

\[E'\le-\frac{2m}{3\gamma}E+\frac{2e\|x\|}{\gamma}+\frac{e^2}{\gamma L}.\]

The error is explicit and vanishes when the average force satisfies the exact sector at the original position difference.

steps.title: Control the actual average of the two nonlinear force evaluations
steps.body: Let \(F,F'\) satisfy the strong-smooth centered bounds at differences \(x,x'\), and set \(S=(F+F')/2\). With \(\mu=(m+L)/2\) and \(R=(L-m)/2\), decompose \(S-\mu x\) into half of each centered force residual plus \(\mu(x'-x)/2\). The triangle inequality and \(\|x'\|\le\|x\|+\|x'-x\|\) yield \(\|S-\mu x\|\le R\|x\|+(L/2)\|x'-x\|\). Thus the sector error is precisely \(e=(L/2)\|x'-x\|\). A centered residual controls monotonicity by Cauchy–Schwarz. Moving its center from \(\mu x\) to \(Lx/2\) and squaring yields the approximate cocoercivity bound needed above. Lean proves both consequences from the explicit norm inequality.

steps.title: Apply the sector proof to the original potential
steps.body: For two arbitrary position pairs, use the project's proved strong-smooth interpolation and centered-ball theorem to obtain the two force residual bounds directly from differentiability, strong convexity and Lipschitz gradient. Their average is exactly the average of the two gradient differences used by the two OBABO kicks. The preceding average-sector lemma supplies the explicit position-increment error, and the perturbed dissipativity theorem supplies the source drift bound. No Hessian regularity, invented secant matrix, or assumed contraction inequality appears in this nonlinear step. The remaining discrete proof must bound the displayed error and the actual integrator remainder using its step-size restrictions.

KineticLangevin/HamiltonianRejection.lea.title: Quadratic rejection mass under a concrete phase moment
KineticLangevin/HamiltonianRejection.lea.summary: The exact Verlet energy defect controls its actual Metropolis rejection probability. For steps between zero and one, the state-dependent bound simplifies to a single quadratic phase envelope. Integrating this bound requires precisely the velocity and force second moments displayed in the theorem, and supplies the vanishing error needed for a fixed-horizon weak limit.

steps.title: Apply the scalar rejection inequality to the actual energy defect
steps.body: The acceptance is defined by the actual defect \(d=H(V_hz)-H(z)\). The already proved scalar inequality \(1-\min\{1,e^{-d}\}\le |d|\) therefore applies by substitution, with no acceptance approximation.

steps.title: Reduce all intermediate stages to a quadratic phase envelope
steps.body: Put \(a=\|v\|\), \(b=\| abla f(x)\|\), \(w=v-h abla f(x)/2\), and \(q=a^2+b^2\). For \(0\le h\le1\), the triangle inequality gives \(\|w\|\le a+b\), hence \(\|w\|^2\le2q\). Also \(2\|w\|b\le\|w\|^2+b^2\), so \(\|w\|(2b+Mh\|w\|)\le(2M+3)q\). Substitution in the earlier exact defect estimate yields \[|H(V_hz)-H(z)|\le h^2 rac{M(2M+11)}8 igl(\|v\|^2+\| abla f(x)\|^2 igr).\] Lean retains the intermediate nonnegative scalar bounds, checks every multiplication by \(h\) and \(M\), and combines them by polynomial arithmetic. The following theorem composes this estimate with the scalar rejection inequality.

steps.title: Integrate the proved rejection envelope
steps.body: For any finite phase measure with integrable \(q(z)=\|v\|^2+\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\), the rejection factor is measurable and lies between zero and one, so it is integrable. The pointwise bound integrates to \[\int(1-a_h)\,d\pi\le h^2\frac{M(2M+11)}8\int q\,d\pi.\] Lean proves bounded integrability of rejection directly from the acceptance bounds and applies monotonicity of the ordinary integral against the explicitly assumed finite quadratic moment. No one-step trajectory or stationary-flow conclusion is supplied as a premise.

KineticLangevin/HamiltonianIteration.lea.title: Linear accumulation of weak error and exact limiting laws
KineticLangevin/HamiltonianIteration.lea.summary: Corrected invariance can be used entirely through bounded tests. Composing a test with more deterministic proposal steps preserves its bound. Each telescoping increment is therefore controlled under the same fixed measure, giving a linear accumulation of rejection mass. Pointwise convergence and vanishing accumulated error then identify the limiting law exactly by dual characteristic functions.

steps.title: Telescope tests composed with deterministic iterates
steps.body: Let \(A_k=\int F(V^kz)\,d\pi\). Apply the one-step weak estimate to \(G=F\circ V^k\). Measurability of iterates proves measurability of \(G\), and the same bound \(\|G\|\le C\) holds. Thus \(\|A_{k+1}-A_k\|\le2C\int(1-a)\,d\pi\). The triangle inequality and induction give \[\|A_n-A_0\|\le2Cn\int(1-a)\,d\pi.\] Lean explicitly rewrites the successor iterate as \(V^k\circ V\), applies the checked one-step result, and normalizes the successor natural-number cast. Every increment is integrated against the fixed measure \(\pi\); no law of an unadjusted intermediate chain is assumed invariant.

steps.title: Identify the actual limiting pushforward through characteristic tests
steps.body: Suppose measurable maps \(Y_n\) converge pointwise to a measurable map \(Y\), and the bounded-test error is eventually at most a real sequence \(\delta_n\to0\). For every continuous real linear functional \(L\), use \(F(z)=\exp(iLz)\), whose norm is one. Dominated convergence under the finite measure gives \(\int F(Y_nz)\,d\pi\to\int F(Yz)\,d\pi\). The error bound gives convergence of the same sequence to \(\int F\,d\pi\). Uniqueness of limits equates the dual characteristic functions of \(Y_\#\pi\) and \(\pi\); the checked uniqueness theorem for finite measures gives \(Y_\#\pi=\pi\). Lean uses dual characteristic functions, so the result applies to Banach phase space with its usual product norm and does not silently require that norm to arise from an inner product.

KineticLangevin/HamiltonianConvergence.l.title: Prove Verlet converges to the actual Hamiltonian flow
KineticLangevin/HamiltonianConvergence.l.summary: Exact reversibility and volume preservation of the Verlet map do not by themselves identify the continuous Hamiltonian flow. This module supplies that analytic limit. For a globally Lipschitz force, the actual Verlet iterates on a mesh of size \(T/(n+1)\) converge to every continuous Hamiltonian integral solution at time \(T\). Specializing to the gradient force identifies the limit with the Picard-selected hamiltonianFlow. The proof uses a genuine local state-error calculation, uniform growth of an Euler comparison chain, a discrete Grönwall estimate, and the existing Euler convergence theorem. It needs no Hessian assumption.

steps.title: Control the elementary shears and their symmetric composition
steps.body:
Use the standard maximum norm on phase pairs \((v,x)\). A kick of duration \(h\ge0\) is \((1+Mh)\)-Lipschitz when the force is \(M\)-Lipschitz, and a drift is \((1+h)\)-Lipschitz. The two half kicks around one drift therefore have factor \((1+Mh/2)^2(1+h)\). For \(0\le h\le1\), expansion and \(h^2,h^3\le h\) bound it by

\[\|\operatorname{Verlet}_h(z)-\operatorname{Verlet}_h(w)\|\le\bigl(1+(M+1)^2h\bigr)\|z-w\|.\]

Lean first bounds the velocity and position projections by the phase norm. It rewrites each difference so the shared force difference is explicit, applies the triangle inequality and the force Lipschitz estimate, and handles the product norm using max_le. The Verlet estimate composes the three bounds; a scalar polynomial inequality controls the resulting product. This is a stability estimate for the actual symmetric map, not an assumed numerical property.

steps.title: Compute and bound the actual local Verlet state defect
steps.body:
Let \(v_{1/2}=v-hg(x)/2\) and \(x_+=x+hv_{1/2}\). Compare Verlet with the explicit Hamiltonian Euler step \((v-hg(x),x+hv)\). Their exact coordinate differences are

\[\Delta v=-\frac h2\bigl(g(x_+)-g(x)\bigr),\qquad\Delta x=-\frac{h^2}{2}g(x).\]

The Lipschitz bound gives \(\|g(x)\|\le(M+1)(\|z\|+\|g(0)\|)\) and \(\|v_{1/2}\|\le(M+2)(\|z\|+\|g(0)\|)\) for \(h\le1\). Consequently,

\[\|\operatorname{Verlet}_h(z)-(z-hD(z))\|\le h^2(M+1)(M+2)(\|z\|+\|g(0)\|),\quad D(v,x)=(g(x),-v).\]

Lean proves the two displayed coordinate identities by module algebra. It then applies the force Lipschitz estimate to \(x_+-x=hv_{1/2}\), rewrites scalar-multiple norms, and bounds each coordinate before taking their maximum. This deliberately sufficient quadratic local estimate proves convergence under only a Lipschitz force; it does not claim a second-order global rate under those minimal assumptions.

steps.title: Bound the entire Euler comparison chain on a fixed horizon
steps.body:
Write \(X_{k+1}=X_k-hd(X_k)\), with \(d\) globally \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(nh=T\). The distance from the actual initial point satisfies

\[e_{k+1}\le(1+Lh)e_k+h\|d(X_0)\|,\qquad e_0=0.\]

The finite recurrence estimate and \((1+Lh)^k\le e^{Lkh}\le e^{LT}\) yield, for every \(k\le n\),

\[\|X_k\|\le\|X_0\|+T\|d(X_0)\|e^{LT}.\]

The bound is uniform over the number of mesh steps. Lean derives the recurrence by comparing one Euler update with the update of the fixed initial point, invoking the previously proved Lipschitz bound for explicit Euler. finite_euler_recurrence_bound sums the recurrence. The inequality \(1+r\le e^r\), the exponential power identity, and the partition equation \(nh=T\) control the amplification. No boundedness of the numerical trajectory is added as a hypothesis.

steps.title: Propagate the local difference between Verlet and Euler
steps.body:
Let \(V_k\) be the actual Verlet iterates and \(X_k\) the actual Euler iterates from the same initial phase. Split their next difference into a Verlet stability term and the local Verlet-versus-Euler defect evaluated at \(X_k\). The proved Euler growth bound makes the local coefficient uniform in \(k\). With \(A=(M+1)^2\) and

\[C=(M+1)(M+2)\bigl(\|z\|+T\|D(z)\|e^{(M+1)T}+\|g(0)\|\bigr),\]

the actual error satisfies \(e_{k+1}\le(1+Ah)e_k+h^2C\), hence

\[\|V_n-X_n\|\le ThC e^{AT}.\]

Lean constructs the two concrete chains and proves their recursive update formulas. The triangle inequality combines the established stability and local-defect theorems. The finite recurrence bound gives \(nh^2C(1+Ah)^n\); the partition identity converts \(nh^2\) into \(Th\), and the exponential bound removes dependence on \(n\). This is the full finite-horizon numerical comparison required by the limit theorem.

steps.title: Send the mesh size to zero
steps.body:
Choose \(h_n=T/(n+1)\). This mesh tends to zero, and eventually \(h_n\le1\), so the finite comparison applies. Its right side is the vanishing mesh times a fixed, finite coefficient depending only on the horizon, force, and initial phase. Therefore the norm of the difference between the two actual endpoints tends to zero.

Lean proves the mesh limit from tendsto_const_div_atTop_nhds_zero_nat, obtains the eventual small-step condition from the neighborhood of zero, and applies squeeze_zero' to the nonnegative error norm. tendsto_iff_norm_sub_tendsto_zero upgrades this scalar estimate to convergence of the phase-vector difference itself.

steps.title: Identify the selected Hamiltonian flow as the numerical limit
steps.body:
The existing Euler theorem states that a globally Lipschitz drift's matching-input Euler approximations converge to every continuous solution of its actual integral equation. Here the additive input is zero and the negative Hamiltonian drift is \(D(v,x)=(g(x),-v)\), which has Lipschitz constant at most \(M+1\). Adding the vanishing Verlet-minus-Euler difference to that convergent Euler endpoint proves convergence of Verlet itself.

For \(g=\nabla f\), the selected hamiltonianFlow is already constructed by Picard from this precise integral equation. kineticFlow_spec supplies its continuity, initialization, and integral identity. The final theorem therefore proves

\[\operatorname{Verlet}_{T/(n+1)}^{\,n+1}(z)\longrightarrow\operatorname{hamiltonianFlow}(f,T,z)(T).\]

Lean invokes additiveEulerChain_tendsto with zero input, combines the two limits using Tendsto.add, and simplifies the exact vector identity \((V_n-X_n)+X_n=V_n\). The specialization unfolds only the zero-friction, unit-inverse-mass flow definition and its normalized zero forcing. Neither the desired numerical convergence nor a stationarity conclusion occurs among the hypotheses.

KineticLangevin/Complexity.lean.title: Explicit accuracy budgets and integer iteration counts
KineticLangevin/Complexity.lean.summary: The paper's step-size and iteration formulas are scalar consequences of its numerical error estimate. This module verifies that implication, retains a stability-compatible bias budget, and rounds the logarithmic threshold to a natural number. It handles zero initial error separately and clips negative logarithmic thresholds at zero. These accuracy corollaries have an explicit error inequality as input; they do not replace the outstanding unconditional stochastic theorem.

steps.title: Replace geometric decay by its exponential envelope
steps.body: For \(\alpha\le1\), the base \(1-\alpha\) is nonnegative. The elementary exponential inequality gives \(1-\alpha\le e^{-\alpha}\). Raising this comparison to a natural power preserves order, so \((1-\alpha)^n\le e^{-\alpha n}\). Lean uses Real.add_one_le_exp, pow_le_pow_left₀, and Real.exp_nat_mul. The lemma itself needs no positive lower bound on \(\alpha\); that requirement enters when dividing the logarithmic threshold.

steps.title: Round the logarithmic threshold and include small initial errors
steps.body:
For initial coupling radius \(D\), define

\[n_0=\left\lceil\max\left\{0,\frac{\log(24D/\varepsilon)}\alpha\right\}\right\rceil.\]

This is a natural number even when the logarithm is negative. If \(\alpha>0\) and \(n\ge n_0\), then \(\alpha n\ge\log(24D/\varepsilon)\). Lean combines the ceiling's lower bound, the right-hand inequality for a maximum, and the cast of the natural comparison, before multiplying by the positive \(\alpha\). The explicit maximum and ceiling handle the initialization-dependent small-error regime and integer rounding.

steps.title: Verify the transient budget only when logarithmic cancellation is valid
steps.body: For \(D>0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), exponentiating the iteration inequality gives \(e^{-\alpha n}\le e^{-\log(24D/\varepsilon)}=\varepsilon/(24D)\). The geometric envelope and multiplication by \(D\) imply \((1-\alpha)^nD\le\varepsilon/24\). Lean proves positivity of the logarithm argument before using Real.exp_log, rewrites the negative exponential as an inverse, and cancels the nonzero factors. Zero initial error is handled by the next theorem without a logarithmic cancellation.

steps.title: Combine the manuscript's 0.94 bias allocation with the transient
steps.body:
Suppose an explicit estimate gives \(E_n\le\sqrt2(1-\alpha)^nD+b\), with \(0<\alpha\le1\), \(D\ge0\), and \(b\le0.94\varepsilon\). When \(D=0\), the bias already gives the conclusion and there is no iteration requirement. Otherwise use the rounded threshold. The exact rational inequality \(\sqrt2\le36/25\) bounds the remaining contribution by \(0.06\varepsilon\), so the total error is at most \(\varepsilon\).

Lean proves the square-root comparison by squaring, splits on zero versus positive initial radius, derives the logarithmic condition in the positive case, and combines the inequalities with nonnegative scalar multiplication. For KLMC, substitute \(\alpha=3mh/(4\gamma)\) and bias \(Mh\sqrt{2p}/m\), with a step size that is the minimum of the stability threshold and bias allowance. The same scalar argument applies to KIPLMC1 with its thermal radius and a separately budgeted concentration term.

KineticLangevin/HamiltonianMoments.lean.title: Gibbs finiteness and the exact phase moment from strong convexity
KineticLangevin/HamiltonianMoments.lean.summary: The weak Hamiltonian limit needs finite mass and an integrable velocity-plus-force quadratic envelope. This module derives both for the actual exponential Hamiltonian density in finite dimensions. It factors that density into a radial Gaussian velocity weight and the potential Gibbs weight, uses existing direct Gaussian-domination estimates, and transfers position moments to force moments by Lipschitz growth.

steps.title: Factor the actual Hamiltonian density
steps.body: Because \(H(v,x)=f(x)+\|v\|^2/2\), the positive exponential weight factors as \(e^{-H(v,x)}=e^{-\|v\|^2/2}e^{-f(x)}\). Therefore its product-Haar weighted measure is the product of the separately weighted velocity and position measures. Lean applies the theorem for products of measures with densities, combines the two nonnegative real weights through ENNReal.ofReal_mul, and checks the exponent identity. Normalization has not been assumed or imposed at this step.

steps.title: Derive finite mass of both factors and their product
steps.body: The velocity weight is the radial Gaussian with precision \(1/2\), whose ordinary integral is finite. The position weight has finite mass by the previously proved strong-convexity Gaussian domination: a supporting quadratic lower bound for \(f\) makes \(e^{-f}\) integrable. Lean converts these finite ordinary integrals to finite extended density integrals, instantiates finite weighted measures, and uses the exact factorization to prove finiteness of the full phase measure.

steps.title: Derive velocity and position second moments before normalization
steps.body: A quadratic factor is absorbed by radial Gaussian decay, so \(\int\|v\|^2e^{-\|v\|^2/2}\,dv<\infty\). The same strong-convexity tail estimate gives \(\int\|x\|^2e^{-f(x)}\,dx<\infty\). Lean uses the ordinary-integral characterization of integration under a density, checks that each exponential density is finite and measurable, and invokes the existing Gaussian-tail estimates. These are actual moments of the unnormalized factors, not moment contracts attached to a stationary process.

steps.title: Transfer position moments to force moments
steps.body: Gradient Lipschitz continuity implies \(\| abla f(x)\|\le M\|x\|+\| abla f(0)\|\). Squaring and using \((a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\) gives \(\| abla f(x)\|^2\le2M^2\|x\|^2+2\| abla f(0)\|^2\). The right-hand side is integrable under the finite position Gibbs weight by its second moment. Lean derives the force growth inequality from the Lipschitz difference bound and triangle inequality, then applies domination by this explicit integrable envelope.

steps.title: Assemble the precise phase envelope needed by the weak limit
steps.body: On the factored finite phase measure, \(\|v\|^2\) is integrable by pulling the velocity moment through the first coordinate, and \(\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\) is integrable by pulling the force moment through the second coordinate. Their sum is exactly the envelope appearing in the rejection theorem. Lean rewrites the phase measure by its proved factorization, supplies finiteness of both factors, and adds these two coordinate integrability results. Thus every tail premise in the later Hamiltonian stationarity limit follows from positive strong convexity and a Lipschitz gradient.

KineticLangevin/HamiltonianStationarity..title: Exact Gibbs invariance of the actual Hamiltonian flow
KineticLangevin/HamiltonianStationarity..summary: This module closes the deterministic Hamiltonian stationarity argument. Explicit corrected Verlet proposals preserve the Gibbs measure exactly. Their rejection probability is quadratically small, while the uncorrected Verlet iterates converge to the actual selected Hamiltonian integral solution. Bounded tests transfer invariance through this limit. The finite-dimensional strong-convexity theorem derives every required tail premise, so its statement assumes no invariant flow, numerical convergence, or error contract.

steps.title: Make the actual endpoint a measurable function of its initial state
steps.body: The constructed kinetic endpoint is jointly continuous in initialization and continuous forcing. Fix zero forcing, friction zero, inverse mass one, and endpoint time \(T\). Composing this joint map with \(z\mapsto(z,0)\) proves continuity of the selected Hamiltonian endpoint. Lean supplies the compact forcing-space zero explicitly and simplifies the composed definition. The endpoint pushforward is therefore a concrete measurable law.

steps.title: Pass exact corrected invariance to the actual integral solution
steps.body: Let \(\pi\) be the actual Hamiltonian weighted measure, \(B=\int(\|v\|^2+\|\nabla f(x)\|^2)\,d\pi\), and \(K=M(2M+11)/8\). Use \(N=n+1\) Verlet steps of size \(h=T/N\). Exact corrected invariance and the iterated bounded-test estimate imply, for \(\|F\|\le1\), \[\left\|\int F(V_h^Nz)\,d\pi-\int F\,d\pi\right\|\le 2N\int(1-a_h)\,d\pi\le\frac{2T^2KB}{N}.\] The mesh is eventually at most one, so the proved quadratic rejection estimate applies; the displayed bound tends to zero. The independently proved numerical theorem gives \(V_{T/N}^Nz\to\Phi_Tz\), where \(\Phi\) is the actual Picard integral solution. The bounded-test limit theorem identifies \((\Phi_T)_\#\pi=\pi\). Lean assembles these actual results, proves the mesh limit, checks nonnegative multipliers, and simplifies the exact scalar bound. It assumes only the finite measure and precisely displayed quadratic moment required by this intermediate general theorem.

steps.title: Discharge every tail premise from the potential assumptions
steps.body: In finite dimensions, positive strong convexity and differentiability make the actual Hamiltonian Gibbs measure finite by the factorization and Gaussian domination proved in the moments module. The globally Lipschitz gradient supplies the finite force second moment, and the thermal velocity factor supplies the velocity second moment. Substituting these checked results into the preceding limit theorem gives exact Hamiltonian Gibbs invariance from the original first-order potential assumptions. The theorem applies to every nonnegative finite horizon. It proves the Hamiltonian subflow; the full friction-and-noise kinetic diffusion additionally needs its thermostat splitting limit.

KineticLangevin/BrownianSegmentEquations.title: The exact Brownian equations on every numerical time interval
KineticLangevin/BrownianSegmentEquations.summary: The numerical method uses fresh correlated noise on each interval \((a,a+t]\). The preceding module constructs those noises on the same canonical Brownian source and proves independence across disjoint intervals. Here the actual noises also satisfy the integrated kinetic equations, so their relationship to the continuous diffusion is an equality in L² rather than a matching-law assumption.

steps.title: Identify the Brownian increment on a translated interval
steps.body: Define \(W^a_t=B_{a+t}-B_a\). The unit response kernel on \((a,a+t]\) is exactly the difference \(1_{(0,a+t]}-1_{(0,a]}\). Lean proves the indicator identity almost everywhere using Lp.ext, the explicit representatives, and real order arithmetic. Linearity of the isonormal Wiener-integral map then identifies its image with the actual Brownian increment. This fixes the driving noise as a constructed object on the original probability space.

steps.title: Integrate the shifted velocity response
steps.body: Write \(V^a_t=\int_a^{a+t}e^{-\gamma(a+t-r)}\,dB_r\) and \(P^a_t=\int_a^{a+t}\psi_1(a+t-r)\,dB_r\). Translation of deterministic time kernels is a continuous linear isometry. Therefore continuity of the unshifted kernels gives continuity of each translated stochastic response in L². The already proved deterministic primitive identity \(K_{\psi_1}(t)=\int_0^tK_{\psi_0}(s)ds\) survives translation and application of the isonormal map. The Lean proof composes their continuous linear maps and invokes intervalIntegral_comp_comm, proving \(P^a_t=\int_0^tV^a_sds\) without pointwise evaluation of an L² class.

steps.title: Prove the actual damped Brownian integral equation
steps.body: The exact coefficient identity \(\psi_0+\gamma\psi_1=1\) gives \(V^a_t+\gamma P^a_t=W^a_t\). Lean first uses injectivity of the isonormal linear isometry to recover the deterministic kernel identity from the unshifted balance, then applies time translation and the same map. Substituting the primitive gives \(V^a_t=W^a_t-\gamma\int_0^tV^a_sds\). This equality supplies the additive forcing needed when a continuous reference trajectory and a numerical step share one Brownian interval.

steps.title: Recover the ordinary Brownian convolution formula
